title: iOS 27 adds scam-prevention feature to iPhone, here’s how to enable it
snippet: iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it.

Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can detect suspicious activity in real time to prevent scams

Every day around the world, people get tricked into sharing sensitive information like bank details or other financial info with bad actors.

This commonly happens via text messages, emails, or phone calls to iPhone or Android devices. And while iOS has built-in tools like call and message screening, those tools can’t prevent a scam if you choose to take action on it.

But iOS 27 introduces a new level of scam-prevention with a security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection.’

Here’s what it does, per Apple’s website:

Impersonation Risk Detection helps protect against active social engineering scams. In these scams, an attacker might pose as a bank, government agency, or someone you trust to pressure or guide you into making a payment or changing your account details. Traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t always detect this kind of scam. That’s because you’re taking the action, even though you’ve been tricked or pressured.

Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes information about your device and Apple Account to help detect signs of an active scam. Based on this analysis, it returns a risk level to the app. The app receives only the risk level, not the underlying information used to generate it. The app decides what to do next. For example, it might ask you to verify your identity, add a delay, or show a warning.

You can turn Impersonation Risk Detection on in iOS 27 by going to Settings ⇾ Privacy & Security ⇾ Impersonation Risk Detection then toggling on ‘Share with App Developers.’

Impersonation Risk Detection is only available in supported apps, and Apple hasn’t published a list of those apps at the moment. But once enabled, it provides the app with a “risk level” while omitting the underlying information driving it. Risk levels include:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected

Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected

High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected

Once the app has this risk level, it decides what action to take. For example, it may prompt you to offer additional authentication, or show a warning message related to scams.

For more details on how the feature works using ‘Trust Insights,’ see our coverage here.

title: Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer
snippet: Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection. more…
fullText:
Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection.

Chrome is adding suspicious site warnings in the address bar “when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites.” There are two tiers:

Suspicious sites (lower confidence verdict, possible risk of user harm)

Dangerous sites (high confidence verdict, high risk of user harm)

Suspicious sites (above) will trigger a shield icon in the Omnibox, with a dialog box letting you “Mark as safe” or go “Back to safety.” 

Dangerous site alerts (below) will continue to appear as a “full-page red interstitial warning.”

	

Meanwhile, Chrome is continuing to boost scam detection by leveraging Gemini models in the cloud after using on-device approaches. This protects Enhanced Protection users from a broader range of threats, including fake antivirus and browser update scams.

This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites.

Safe Browsing uses the Gemini analysis “in combination with domain reputation and other security signals.” Google will process page content ephemerally, “meaning it is never logged, retained, or used to train models.”

The final Enhanced Protection update defends against ClickFix social engineering that “tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands on their own computers in order to ‘fix’ a fake issue.” In reality, this is used to “carry out malicious actions such as downloading and setting up malware.”

Because these utilities are native to the system and trusted by security software, bad actors use them to blend in and hide their activity, and by shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.

When a potential ClickFix script is copied, Chrome will remove personally identifiable information from the clipboard and send it to Safe Browsing for further analysis. The browser shows a warning if a “dangerous verdict is returned.”

This system is designed to be high precision, in order to protect users in real time while minimizing disruption to legitimate developer activity.

Enhanced Protection was introduced in 2020, and Google said it was enabled by 1 billion users in 2025. It can be enabled in Chrome Settings > Privacy and security > Security.

title: Perplexity’s Computer can now run entirely on your Mac, even offline
snippet: Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection. more…
fullText:
Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection.

Perplexity brings fully local AI tasks to Mac with new Computer mode option

The launch follows Hybrid Compute, which arrived in September. That feature splits tasks between cloud models for research and reasoning and a local model for working with private files.

Local-first takes things further by running both the AI model and the agent directing the task on the Mac.

Perplexity says planning, reasoning, and file processing can all happen on device, with files only reaching the cloud when the user approves.

With permission, Computer can work with local files and supported Mac apps, including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers.

Perplexity Computer can now run fully local on your Mac.

Work with your native Mac apps and local files, and run tasks without sending sensitive data to the cloud. The model and the agent both run on your Mac.

Available now in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/tnvCgCXD7v

— Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) October 20, 2026

One example Perplexity gives is reviewing recent messages and emails, identifying deadlines, and creating an action list in Notes.

Users can still authorize cloud access when a task needs current information, browser use, or connected apps. Hybrid Compute also remains available in the same Mac app.

The new local mode is available to Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. 

It launches with Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro as local model options, which users can download and set up through the app.

You need an Apple silicon Mac with at least 36GB of unified memory for the best experience. You can learn more about the latest Perplexity Computer upgrade here.

title: Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months
snippet: Xbox's first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. fullText:
Xbox’s first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today, according to an internal Xbox memo seen by The Verge. Chiang has been at Microsoft for 21 years, serving as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox chief operating officer in July.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Chiang’s departure in a surprisingly short memo today. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” said Sharma. As Chiang is departing today, her immediate responsibilities are being split up between other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma notes that “We’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”

That sounds like the COO position isn’t going away after just a few months, but it’s not clear why Chiang is departing after such a short stint in the role. At the time of Chiang’s promotion, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described the new chief operating officer role as a first for Xbox, “with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.” The role was created as part of Xbox’s big “reset.”

Chiang reported directly to Sharma, and was promoted to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Chiang departs amid rumors that Xbox is preparing more layoffs this month, in November, and January. The sudden and short memo from Sharma, coupled with Chiang’s responsibilities being assigned to other Xbox leaders, makes it seem like this wasn’t a resignation.

I asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s departure, and the company refused to discuss the circumstances of her exit. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,” says Kari Perez, Xbox vice president of communications. “We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

title: My experience suggests Apple Glasses will only sell to existing eyeglasses wearers
snippet: No, I haven’t managed to get my hands on a prototype pair of Apple Glasses, but I now have experience of the rough equivalents of what we’re expecting from both a 1st- and 2nd-gen product. In both cases, I could definitely see attractions, and I would absolutely upgrade to smart glasses if I wore conventional eyeglasses. But as someone who doesn’t, I can’t see the technology persuading me to do so … more…
fullText:
No, I haven’t managed to get my hands on a prototype pair of Apple Glasses, but I now have experience of the rough equivalents of what we’re expecting from both a 1st- and 2nd-gen product.

In both cases, I could definitely see attractions, and I would absolutely upgrade to smart glasses if I wore conventional eyeglasses. But as someone who doesn’t, I can’t see the technology persuading me to do so …

1st-gen Apple Glasses

The first-gen Apple Glasses expected to launch next year will not have a display, only audio output. It will be something akin to Ray-Ban Meta glasses, only probably without the photo and video capabilities. The camera will only be used to power the Visual Intelligence features. 

Personally, I see this primarily as a stepping stone to a later, more sophisticated product with built-in displays. When I used the AI features in the Meta glasses, I found it very technologically impressive, but the novelty wore off very quickly and I didn’t find many practical uses.

The usefulness of this device will depend very much on the Apple Intelligence capabilities. I’ll certainly be interested to see whether Apple can make a convincing case for the first-gen device, but I find it very hard indeed to imagine the company would persuade non-eyeglass wearers to buy them.

2nd-gen Apple Glasses

The next generation, however, is expected to have a display. As a preview of this experience, I’ve been testing the Even Realities G2 smart glasses. 

I said when I first tried them that they are an extremely impressive piece of technology. They really do feel like something from the future, and friends who’ve tried them have said the same. 

At the time I began testing them, the UK was in the middle of a heat wave, so I was wearing sunglasses full time while outside anyway, and given how light these are, there was absolutely no downside to using these instead. 

Again, the AI features give great demo and feel very sci-fi, but I didn’t really find much practical use for them. Instead, I found the glasses great for three things:

Notifications

Navigation

Translation

My question at the time was what would happen when autumn arrived and I wouldn’t otherwise be wearing any kind of glasses? Would the benefits prove sufficient that I would wear them anyway?

For notifications, the answer is absolutely not. Yes, when I’m wearing them anyway, it’s extremely convenient to simply see a notification appear mid-air in front of me without having to look at a watch or pull out an iPhone. But I don’t allow many notifications, and unless you’re receiving a constant stream of important ones throughout your day, I can’t see anyone wearing smart glasses just for this. 

For navigation, my answer is yes … but the occasions on which this would be beneficial are relatively infrequent. The biggest benefit is when visiting an unfamiliar city, when it’s very welcome indeed, as it enables extremely easy navigation while still being able to enjoy all of the sights around you. In my hometown of London, it sometimes proved useful when walking or cycling to an unfamiliar place, but this was typically no more than two or three times a month. 

The single best application in my view is the translation feature. It’s absolutely fantastic to be able to be making eye contact with someone and to get an instant visual translation. I find this way better than all audio translation in my ears. Of course, unless they have a pair too, then the benefit is limited as they will need to be either listening or looking down at the phone when I’m speaking. But of course, that too is a rather infrequent need for most of us.

Who will buy them?

I think even if you don’t currently wear eyeglasses, if you travel frequently to a wide range of unfamiliar foreign cities, then smart glasses with a display make perfect sense. Between the navigation and translation features, I would view the purchase as a no-brainer. However, while that was once my life, back in my tech research days, that’s not the case today.

	

Maybe if I wore eyeglasses and could justify the cost for the gadget factor and a bit of convenience, then I might shrug and say, why not? If your prescription is stable and you’re going to be able to use them for a number of years, then perhaps even relatively mild benefits would sell them.

But I would say for most people who don’t currently wear eyeglasses, they would be a very tough sell. If you’re not constantly being bombarded with notifications, aren’t often navigating to unfamiliar places, and don’t frequently have the need to understand people speaking a language you don’t speak yourself, then smart glasses like this are just very impressive technology that will spend most of their time gathering dust in a drawer.

Of course, Apple may pull something out of the hat here, just as it did with the iPhone Duo. The company took a form factor that was cute but compromised and appears to have turned it into a must-have device for a significant number of people. Perhaps it will do the same with Apple Glasses. Right now, however, my view is that if you wear eyeglasses and can afford them, you’ll probably want the 2nd-gen. If you don’t, then I can’t currently, well, see it.

What’s your view? Do you think Apple will come up with a killer app for either 1st- or 2nd-gen glasses, or simply implement the technology so well that you’d be willing to wear a pair routinely? Or do you think they will only sell to those who already wear eyeglasses? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Spotify’s ‘QR code verification’ cracks down on sharing and could ban you for a year
snippet: Spotify is rolling out a new method of cracking down on Family plan sharing, with “QR code verification” that’s not particularly hard to work around, but has major consequences if you miss the window. more…
fullText:
Spotify is rolling out a new method of cracking down on Family plan sharing, with “QR code verification” that’s not particularly hard to work around, but has major consequences if you miss the window.

Spotify confirms it won’t stop Family Plan sharing verification, but it’s not a ‘crackdown’

Cracking down on password and/or account sharing has become very common in the world of streaming subscriptions, and Spotify is now trying a new method of limiting the use of its Family plan through a new method – QR code verification.

Spotify details this on a support page, explaining that Family plan members may need to “verify they live with the plan manager by scanning a QR code.” The code appears on the device of the plan manager and is scannable following a pop-up that appears on the device of members of the plan.

Spotify explains the process:

	

The plan manager opens the QR code on their phone. Find it by tapping your profile picture, then Your Premium, then Manage.

The plan member scans the QR code with their phone camera.

Both the manager and member need to be in the same place to complete the scan.

Users on Reddit spotted this rolling out, adding that the QR code changes “every few seconds.” That makes it harder for a screenshot of the page to be used to complete the process. Some quickly found that using multiple devices and video calls, though, they could work around the process. 

Image via Reddit

Spotify says that users have a 7-day window between when the QR code prompt first appears to complete the verification process. Spotify’s Family plan terms require users to live in the same household. 

	

If you miss the 7-day window for scanning the QR code, the consequences are major. Spotify says that users that miss the window “can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months,” but can still sign up for their own Individual plan. Otherwise, they’re automatically pushed down to the free plan as soon as the window closes.

Plan members have 7 days to complete the QR code scan after getting the notification.

If a member misses the window or can’t complete verification:

They can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months

They can choose a different plan at www.spotify.com/premium

The same 12-month sharing ban is imposed on address checks that Spotify has used in the past, but the QR code method is significantly harder to get around.

snippet: Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … more…
fullText:
Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. In all, it says that nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states.

The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … 

	

Apple today announced one new partnership and a second expanded one through the American Manufacturing Program (AMP).

Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made […]

“We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.”

The company says it’s committing up to $100 million over the next three years to assist Perryman in making the grade 5 titanium used in the enclosure for the iPhone Duo. It says Qnity Electronics will be making a component used in the variable aperture lens of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. 

Apple highlighted the work performed by five additional US suppliers:

Broadcom is expanding and modernizing its Fort Collins, Colorado, facility under a $1.5 billion capital investment announced in July, producing advanced radio frequency components for a wide range of Apple products. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips.

Corning, an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility.

Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. This technology enables Face ID and other key features across iPhone and iPad, including the redesigned, even more useful Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

TSMC’s Arizona fab continues to scale its production of advanced chips used across a range of Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch — producing more than 100 million chips for Apple in 2026. Construction on the north campus is progressing as Apple’s partnership with TSMC in Arizona grows.

Amkor Technology broke ground on its first high-volume packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona, in September 2025, and began shell construction earlier this year. Phases 1 and 2 of the project are expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 local hires. Apple will be one of the facility’s first customers, marking another step toward expanding the scope of U.S. advanced manufacturing.

The iPhone maker says the new partnerships include increased use of recycled materials, and that all of its direct suppliers are required to power their entire Apple manufacturing operations with renewable energy by the end of the decade.

title: iOS 27.1 is exclusive to iPhone Duo, here’s why
snippet: iOS 27.1 has officially launched, but you wouldn’t know it by checking your iPhone’s Settings app. That’s because the latest iPhone update is exclusive to iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.1 has officially launched, but you wouldn’t know it by checking your iPhone’s Settings app. That’s because the latest iPhone update is exclusive to iPhone Duo.

iPhone Duo is only model getting iOS 27.1, with all other iPhones skipping to iOS 27.2

Last night, Apple quietly released a major new software update for iPhone.

iOS 27.1 was pushed out over the air, and normally that would mean new features for everyone.

However, you won’t find iOS 27.1 by opening the Settings app and navigating to General ⇾ Software Update. Instead, iOS 27.0.1 will appear as the most recent update.

That’s because iOS 27.1 is exclusive to the new iPhone Duo.

It’s an unusual move, but Apple decided to skip iOS 27.1 for most iPhone models and go straight to iOS 27.2 instead.

iOS 27.2 has been in beta testing for the last month and ships to all users next week. It includes new features like:

Messages: Suggested Actions

Apple Music: New app icon and updated design

Apple TV: User profiles

Apple Podcasts: Overhauled Up Next queue

FaceTime: Dual Capture for group calls

Siri AI: More languages supported

So why did Apple ship iOS 27.1 for iPhone Duo only?

Even though the iPhone Duo was officially unveiled last month, there are plenty of features and details we’ve only recently learned about. Bypassing a beta cycle for iOS 27.1 meant Apple was able to keep many of those details hidden until the Duo’s official launch.

Additionally, there were likely engineering reasons why it was simpler on Apple’s end to keep iOS 27.1 separate and Duo-exclusive. There are all kinds of custom iOS designs and features that the Duo introduces, and it’s expected that managing all of that internally was easier without other models or new features in the mix.

So next week when your iPhone says iOS 27.2 is available to install, just know that you didn’t somehow miss iOS 27.1 entirely.

Wireless Fast Charging

a MagSafe Charger (currently only $30)

That said, the Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter at its reduced price is a great deal for a first-party option.

title: The Boox Palma 2 Pro finally got me to stop reading on my phone
snippet: The $400 Boox Palma 2 Pro is a smartphone-sized e-reader designed for people who want to read books, articles, and documents on a small E Ink display.
fullText:
The $400 Boox Palma 2 Pro is a smartphone-sized e-reader designed for people who want to read books, articles, and documents on a small E Ink display. However, it offers more than just a dedicated reading experience because it runs Android and supports Google Play, giving you access to third-party apps. Think of it as a cross between a Kindle and a compact Android tablet. 

What drew me to reviewing the Palma 2 Pro was its size. When I’m not reading a physical book, I like to lie on my side and read at night before bed. Most e-readers are squarish and hard to hold without something like a PopSocket, and they can feel too big for reading while lying down. So even though I own a Kindle, I often ended up reading on my iPhone simply because it was more comfortable in my hand. But, reading on your phone for too long can of course cause eye strain. The Palma 2 Pro ultimately solved this problem for me during the two months I spent testing it.

The device’s front-lit screen lets you choose between cool and warm lighting. This was a big plus for me because when I’m reading in bed at night, I don’t want to disturb my sleeping husband with the light. While you can lower the brightness on a smartphone, the Palma 2 Pro can be dimmed to an exceptionally low level. Even when reading in complete darkness, I could see the screen clearly without straining my eyes or disturbing my husband.

Not only was the Boox Palma 2 Pro easier on my eyes, but it was also noticeably lighter than my iPhone, weighing just 175 grams and making it even more comfortable to hold.

Image Credits:Boox /

And since it’s pocket-sized, I ended up carrying it everywhere, from the doctor’s office to the airport, especially since it fits in my small, everyday purse that isn’t big enough for a Kindle. So, in moments when I would normally scroll on my phone, I was getting some reading in instead. 

Since it’s not a locked-down e-reader, you can download apps like Kindle, Kobo, and Libby, as well as apps for audiobooks, podcasts, read-it-later services, and email. This means that you don’t have to use the built-in reader app, and can choose to read on your preferred app. 

Access to apps turns the compact E Ink device into a versatile tool for reading, research, and productivity. It’s worth noting that while scrolling through these apps, animations and some interfaces may feel sluggish because not all apps are optimized for E Ink. And while the device is capable of displaying color, images will definitely look less vibrant than they would a smartphone screen.

For me, the Palma 2 Pro became a dedicated device for reading and listening to audiobooks, which allowed me to enjoy the best of both worlds without the usual distractions that come with a smartphone.

The Boox Palma 2 Pro also features a rear camera for scanning documents, a built-in speaker for listening to audio without headphones, and a hybrid SIM slot for cellular data on the go.

Image Credits:Boox /

The device is compatible with a stylus, so you can take notes and mark up PDFs. However, I can’t speak to that experience since I didn’t receive a stylus with my review unit. 

As for battery life, the device lasted about 5–7 days, which worked for me but could be a downside for people who are used to Kindles, which can last for weeks on a single charge. Additionally, if you want to get more juice out of the device, you can just turn off Wi-Fi. 

One downside I found, especially for an e-reader at this price point, is that there’s quite a bit of ghosting. Text from a previous page can linger on the screen when you turn to the next page or return to the home screen. There’s a refresh button in the navigation bar that quickly clears it, but it may get annoying for some users to repeatedly have to do that.

I think the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great device for a very specific type of reader: someone who wants a smartphone-sized device for comfort, portability, as well as access to apps. If you’re someone who loves your Kindle, I don’t think this device is for you. But if, like me, you’re tired of reading on your phone and dealing with eye strain or headaches, the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great option.

Of course, the price is quite steep for an e-reader, so you’ll have to decide whether the added versatility and portability are worth the extra cost. It’s worth mentioning that Boox is launching a non-Pro Palma 3 soon for $340 that features a black and white display and replaces the Palma 2.

title: iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new feature from the Mac
snippet: iPadOS 27.2 launches next week, and among its many new features, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac addition: a Siri popup when text is selected. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 launches next week, and among its many new features, Apple has also brought over a recent Mac addition: a Siri popup when text is selected.

Siri AI is the tentpole addition to iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and companion releases. And as such, Apple offers lots of ways to access the new, supercharged assistant.

On iPad you can invoke Siri via a “Siri” or “Hey Siri” voice prompt, pull down from the top of the screen, use the new Siri option in the edit menu, open the new Siri app, or my personal favorite: use CMD + Space to open Spotlight and ask Siri a question from there.

But iPadOS 27.2 adds yet another option that’s borrowed directly from the Mac.

In macOS 27 Golden Gate, in many situations when you select some text, a small Siri icon appears in the top-left corner of the selection. When you hover over the icon with your cursor, it expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text box.

This wasn’t available in iPadOS 27. But now, if you have a trackpad connected to your iPad, that same behavior is available in iPadOS 27.2.

As seen in the images above, the new Siri icon starts out small and stays out of the way, but it’s very convenient to just hover over it to make the ‘Ask Siri’ box appear.

If you don’t have a trackpad attached, selecting text will still reveal the full edit menu where you can tap to open Siri. But it’s a more smooth and seamless experience with a trackpad.

macOS is full of small productivity-focused features like this that speed up everyday interactions, yet are missing from iPadOS. So it’s exciting to see such a recent Mac feature be brought over to the iPad.

title: Orangetheory adds Apple Watch in-studio workout tracking for a one-time fee
snippet: Starting tomorrow, Orangetheory Fitness will allow members to connect the Apple Watch to the club’s proprietary in-studio performance-tracking experience. Using a personal Apple Watch with the Orangetheory system will require a one-time fee. more…
fullText:
Starting tomorrow, Orangetheory Fitness will allow members to connect the Apple Watch to the club’s proprietary in-studio performance-tracking experience. Using a personal Apple Watch with the Orangetheory system will require a one-time fee.

OTconnect for Apple Watch launches for $99 on October 23

“The new option, called OTconnect for Apple Watch, is part of Orangetheory’s proprietary connected technology platform, which tracks real-time performance and delivers post-class results,” Orangetheory Fitness announced today. 

Connecting a personal Apple Watch to the Orangetheory system will require a one-time $99 fee, the fitness club says. Apple Watch connectivity is optional and joins the existing OTconnect Beat solution for Orangetheory’s connected system.

“For a one-time $99 connection fee, members can now use their Apple Watch during an Orangetheory class to access real-time performance data, including calories burned, heart rate and heart rate zones displayed directly on the wrist, in addition to Splat Points.”

The company shares more details about how the OTConnect for Apple Watch system will work.

“Before class, members can start their workout on Apple Watch once it connects to OTconnect. After class, they can review their performance summary directly in the app on Apple Watch, with additional workout data and personalized insights available through the OTF app and via email post-class.”

This marks Orangetheory’s second Apple Watch integration

Orangetheory previously introduced Apple Watch integration in 2019 through its OTbeat Link accessory. The $129 device attached to an Apple Watch band and connected the watch to the company’s in-studio heart rate monitoring system.

The new OTconnect integration eliminates the need for that extra hardware, which was discontinued around 2022.

In addition to unlocking OTConnect for Apple Watch, the one-time charge also includes two more perks with “up to two free months of Apple Music and Apple Fitness+.”

“OTconnect for Apple Watch requires watchOS 11.6 or later and will be available for Apple Watch Series 6 or later, Apple Watch SE or later, and Apple Watch Ultra or later,” the company says. You can read the announcement in full here.

The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are both available now.

title: Four advantages MacBook Pro redesign will have over current model
snippet: Next week Apple will unveil its first MacBook Pro redesign in five years. Rumors indicate the new MacBook Pro will have the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as current models, but with exclusive advantages in at least four other areas. more…
fullText:
Next week Apple will unveil its first MacBook Pro redesign in five years. Rumors indicate the new MacBook Pro will have the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as current models, but with exclusive advantages in at least four other areas.

#1: Significantly lighter industrial design

While the new MacBook Pro design is expected to be a little thinner than the current model, its biggest design advantage is a weight reduction. Per Mark Gurman:

The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

If you’re worried about Apple removing ports with its MacBook Pro redesign, it sounds like the company probably learned its lesson from previous generations. Since the design isn’t expected to slim down too much, it’s likely there will be minimal changes to ports.

#2: OLED display

The Liquid Retina XDR display on current MacBook Pros is an excellent display. But Apple plans to make its new MacBook Pro display even better by introducing OLED.

OLED has been used in iPhones for years, but the only example of Apple using it on larger displays is the iPad Pro. The tandem OLED introduced on iPad in 2024 was touted by Apple as “the world’s most advanced display.”

Now, OLED is coming to the Mac with the new MacBook Pro. And if it’s anything like what the iPad Pro offers, the new display is bound to impress.

#3: Touch support

Most MacBook Pro users probably aren’t asking for touch support. But if you’re like me, you may find that there are some cases where it would be valuable if you could touch the Mac’s display.

Apple’s new MacBook Pro will make that possible. Its OLED display will include full touchscreen capabilities and benefit from touch optimizations throughout macOS Golden Gate.

Touch isn’t replacing the primary input methods of trackpad and keyboard. Rather, it’s being introduced as a secondary “nice-to-have” option.

#4: Notch-free display

Apple’s last MacBook Pro redesign in 2021 brought the notch to the Mac. And this redesign will reportedly remove it.

	

Like Apple has done on the iPhone, it’s removing the notch first on its Pro line. The new MacBook Pro drops the notch, reportedly in favor of a hole-punch camera cutout.

A new Dynamic Island feature is expected to be introduced too, though there’s a chance it might come to older Macs via a software update.

fullText:
iOS 27.2 launches next week with a variety of new features, and also design changes for select Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming.

#1: Apple Music

Apple Music just rolled out a big design rebrand, and iOS 27.2 extends that fresh visual identity to several aspects of the Music app.

For starters, there’s a new app icon that strips the old red color in favor of black and white. The removal of the old red identity extends to other elements inside the app too.

In Music’s tab bar, the accent color for the active tab is now blue instead of red. And in your Library, sections like Playlists, Artists, and Albums are entirely monochrome.

If you use the Music app’s widgets on your Home Screen or Today view, you’ll notice that they drop the former red background too. Now all widgets use a black background instead.

#2: Apple Books

Apple’s Books app in iOS 27.2 introduces design updates centered around its reading experience.

As explained in-depth here, design changes include:

Progress bars are now available to track your reading location

Menu in the bottom-right has a new icon and is a standard Liquid Glass menu for consistency with other apps

Bookmark has been removed from that menu and now lives in the upper-right of the reader view as a standalone button

‘X’ button has moved to the upper-left corner

‘Back’ button has moved to lower-left and is larger than before

These changes were likely motivated by the iPhone Duo’s introduction. 

Not only does the Duo make a great e-reader, but it’s also a reason to avoid bespoke UI elements for things like menus and buttons, since Apple’s stock options dynamically reposition for different iPhone models in a way the old Books controls likely wouldn’t have.

title: Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence
snippet: Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in). more…
fullText:
Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in).

Like in the Gemini app or AI Mode, Personal Intelligence taps into your Google Workspace (including Gmail and Calendar), Photos, Maps, Search, and YouTube to personalize responses. Your prompts and commands don’t have to include specifics as Personal Intelligence can pull those details from emails, photos, or a “place you saved in Google Maps.”

This allows for complex or natural queries, like “What’s my flight gate? And is my flight on time?” or “Take me to my doctor’s appointment.”

“You don’t have to hunt for the confirmation email, then do a separate search for delays. Gemini gives you both answers in one go.”

“You don’t have to remember the street address or look it up before you drive.”

Additionally, Gemini is aware of your preferences when you say: “Find me an indoor restaurant along my route that matches my usual vibe.” This saves you from having to specify you’re vegetarian with every command.

	

Other examples include:

Retrieve details without pulling over: Trying to return to a place you saw earlier? Say, “Find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” You don’t need to scroll through your camera roll or pull over to get the name and directions. 

Pick up where you left off: Heading out for the morning? Say, “Take me to the coffee shop we were talking about yesterday”. Gemini will handle the digging and send you on your way.

	

On the privacy front, Personal Intelligence is opt-in, though it will come to Android Auto automatically if you enabled it for the Gemini app on your phone.

If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you.

Meanwhile, on Android Automotive, Personal Intelligence will only share personalized responses “when you’re in the car with your phone connected.” 

Personal Intelligence is rolling out starting today to Android Auto, with Android Automotive availability in the coming months.

title: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs.

Apple touts Siri AI with personal context and conversational abilities as essential to HomeView

In November 2024, Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on the product we now know as HomeView. At the time, he said Apple was targeting a March 2025 launch. But that date kept slipping, and now HomeView will finally arrive in homes on November 13, 2026.

Why the long wait? Gurman has repeatedly pointed to Siri AI as the chief cause of delays. And Apple execs have now largely confirmed that in quotes given to The Verge.

Jennifer Pattison Tuohy asked Kaiann Drance, Apple’s VP of product marketing for home, why now was the right time for HomeView and Apple’s renewed smart home push.

She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.

HomeView is being marketed as a shared device that taps into users’ personal context in a way that wasn’t possible pre-Siri AI. So it’s easy to see how Apple’s main pitch would need to change without the more personalized Siri.

A similar explanation was given by Apple’s Lilian Rincon, VP of product marketing for AI. She told The Verge that Siri AI is core to HomeView because it’s “much more capable” and also highlighted its conversational abilities, which make it easy to use for any family member.

“It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”

	

This emphasis and explanation also makes HomeView’s absence in the EU more understandable. 

If Siri AI was simply a nice-to-have addition to an otherwise feature-rich product, perhaps it could launch in the EU still. But if the whole value proposition revolves around the new assistant and its personalized features, waiting until Siri AI is available for iOS in the EU makes more sense.

You can read The Verge’s full article here for more quotes and context.

title: Galaxy S27 might drop to 8GB of RAM; other Android phones could go back to 4GB
snippet: As the AI industry continues to directly cause a crisis in the availability of RAM, new rumors suggest that the Galaxy S27 could downgrade to 8GB of RAM, while other Android brands could go back to 4GB for some models. more…
fullText:
As the AI industry continues to directly cause a crisis in the availability of RAM, new rumors suggest that the Galaxy S27 could downgrade to 8GB of RAM, while other Android brands could go back to 4GB for some models.

RAM allotments in modern smartphones are fairly predictable. 12GB or 16GB in a high-end flagship, at least 8GB in most mid-range devices, and around 6GB in most entry-level devices. 4GB isn’t uncommon in entry-level devices, but even the most affordable models have pushed to 6GB in recent years because, frankly, Android just doesn’t run all that well on 4GB anymore. 

But everyone is feeling the strain of the rapidly rising cost of memory. A recent report even claims that Samsung doesn’t make a profit when it sells a Galaxy device.

With that in mind, it’s not entirely surprising to hear that Samsung is considering a downgrade for its upcoming Galaxy S27 series. Leaker and analyst @kro_roe on Twitter/X says that the Galaxy S27 series will see its base models start with 8GB of RAM rather than the 12GB that’s been standard for the past two generations. Specifically, Galaxy S25 and Galaxy S26 both start with 12GB of RAM, with a 16GB option for select trims of the Ultra model.

	

This latest leak shows configurations with 8GB of RAM as the starting amount, and 12GB across the Pro and Ultra tiers.

Galaxy S27: 8GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB

Galaxy S27+: 8GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB

Galaxy S27 Pro: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, 16GB “under consideration”

Galaxy S27 Ultra: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, 16GB/1TB

	

The same leaker says the price increases “may be unavoidable” and that promos like doubled storage may not show up during the pre-order period. Meanwhile, the actual storage type could also differ, with some models “differentiating UFS storage versions” to balance costs. Galaxy S26 used UFS 4.0 across the board.

Samsung might not be alone in these downgrades. Another leaker on Weibo claims that “several” other Android brands are dropping their “top-of-the-line” devices to 12GB, their “main” mid-range models to 8GB, and entry-level devices to 6GB as the “top-of-the-line” offering, with most of those lower-cost Android phones going back to just 4GB of RAM.

It’s hard to know for certain what the future holds at this point, as “RAMageddon” rages on. All we know is that everything is getting more expensive. Thanks AI.

title: From Toast to Bessemer: Who founders will hear from at TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026
snippet: Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs.
fullText:
Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers. 

When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation? 

On November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 will bring together founders, investors, and operators who have tackled those questions from different sides of the table. 

Hosted by TechCrunch in partnership with Fidelity Private Shares, the full-day event goes beyond fundraising and AI to explore the realities of finding customers, building teams, sharpening a pitch, developing founder leadership, and scaling companies both inside and outside traditional startup hubs. Save 25% on your ticket today, and bring a colleague along for free with our limited BOGO deal. 

Some of the speakers founders will hear from in Boston

Steve Fredette on building a company that keeps reinventing itself 

Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers. 

Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.” 

Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company. 

But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place. 

Kent Bennett on knowing when product-market fit is real 

Growth can be exciting. Growing too early can be expensive. 

Kent Bennett, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow? 

The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts. 

It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there. 

Image Credits:Halo Creative / Flickr (opens in a new window)

Rudina Seseri on when to scale and when to hit the brakes 

That same tension takes center stage with Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures. 

In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business. 

Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in. 

Lior Div on building for AI from day one 

AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start. 

Lior Div, CEO and co-founder of 7AI, will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.” 

For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company. 

Chase Garbarino on the Boston founder playbook 

The startup world does not begin and end in Silicon Valley. 

Chase Garbarino, CEO and co-founder of HqO, will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston. 

For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area. 

Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it. 

Dave Balter on the pitch that gets you another meeting 

A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation. 

Dave Balter, venture partner at True Ventures and CEO of Edisyl, will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.” 

For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills. 

Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice. 

Catch the full list of Founders Summit speakers here.

Watch founders pitch live 

At “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders will put their stories to the test live on the Build Stage. 

Balter will be joined by Chirag Shah, partner at Define Ventures, and Simran Suri, principal at Maveron, as startups make their cases in front of an investor judging panel. 

For attendees, it is an opportunity to watch what happens when founders have limited time to make an idea connect, and to hear how investors react in real time. 

It is one of the most interactive parts of the Founder Summit program and a chance to learn from both the pitches that land and the ones that leave questions unanswered. 

More than one startup conversation 

The rest of the program stretches across many of the decisions founders are facing right now. 

Hunter Worland of NEA will explore why distribution may become a startup’s next competitive advantage. Vineet Edupuganti, co-founder and CEO of Cogent Security, will discuss building 10x teams. Tina Tosukhowong of TDK Ventures will examine the hidden signals that can identify category winners. 

Fidelity Private Shares will also bring its perspective to conversations about fundraising trends with Kristen Craft and enterprise relationships with Evan Schnidman. 

Together, the agenda creates a day that is not just about raising the next round or chasing the latest AI trend but is also about building the company. 

Join the conversation in Boston 

TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 takes place November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston. 

The day brings together candid founder conversations, practical sessions, smaller roundtables, live pitching, networking, and a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares. 

With the event approaching quickly and only so many spots left, don’t wait to register! Act now on our limited time offer and save 25% on your Founder Summit ticket.

title: Apple says developers are showing ‘incredible’ support for the iPhone Duo
snippet: One of the major issues raised by early reviews of the iPhone Duo is limited support by third-party apps. As we noted in our own review, there are three tiers of support currently, the worst of which sees an iPhone app stranded in the center of a mostly black area of the display. The good news is that Apple says the position is changing rapidly, citing “incredible” support for the larger display of the folding iPhone … more…
fullText:
One of the major issues raised by early reviews of the iPhone Duo is limited support by third-party apps. As we noted in our own review, there are three tiers of support currently, the worst of which sees an iPhone app stranded in the center of a mostly black area of the display. 

The good news is that Apple says the position is changing rapidly, citing “incredible” support for the larger display of the folding iPhone …

Apple says developers are taking advantage of the flexibility of the iPhone Duo in order to create exciting new experiences.

With an inner display that’s 50 percent larger than iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the flexibility to use iPhone Duo in a variety of poses, developers are enhancing their apps to create exciting new experiences for capturing and sharing memories, streaming entertainment, gaming, multitasking, and much more […]

“The response to iPhone Duo from our developer community has been incredible, and we’re inspired by how quickly they’ve embraced its larger display and new ways to interact,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations. “From watching popular shows and content on the expansive inner display to multitasking across windows or playing console-quality games, developers around the world are reimagining what their apps can do. We can’t wait for users to discover these experiences beginning this Friday, with many more app experiences to follow.”

The company says it will be highlighting some of the best iPhone Duo apps and games on the App Store tomorrow when the new device goes on sale. Apple has already named some of them, starting with streaming video services.

 Netflix makes finding great entertainment even more fun: Members can scroll through Clips on the outer display and then open iPhone Duo to keep watching on the large nano-texture inner display, with Clips switching seamlessly between a vertical or horizontal view.

More streaming services — including Prime Video and Paramount+ — are joining Apple TV in using the larger canvas for movies and series. With iPhone Duo, Prime Video enhances the viewing experience for users as they stream premium entertainment, and when partially folded, content plays on the top half of the display while X-Ray details showing cast and bonus content appear on the bottom half. Paramount+ offers richer playback controls and expanded browsing for shows and live channels.

Two key sports apps have also been updated to take advantage of the new opportunities.

When iPhone Duo is propped open on a table, users can easily enjoy content hands-free, without a stand. Sports fans can follow MLBand PGA Tour with live games and highlights, plus real-time scores, stats, and leaderboards on the larger display.

“Baseball fans are incredibly passionate about the sport, and they follow our games as closely as they can. Now, iPhone Duo provides an exciting new fan engagement platform by showcasing the action and information simultaneously,” said Kenny Gersh, MLB’s executive vice president of Media, Business Development, and Product. “This incredible device unlocks a fun, versatile way to experience baseball from anywhere, and we’re grateful to have worked with Apple to ensure the app is ready for the World Series. Set iPhone Duo on a table partially folded and the live game plays on the upright half of the display while real-time stats fill the half resting on the table, so fans never have to choose between the broadcast and the box score.”

	

Apple says that Microsoft Word and Outlook will roll out a desktop-class experience in the next few weeks, while Zoom, Slack, and Salesforce are also prepping their own updates.

Zoom turns the inner display into an immersive video conference room, so users can see shared content and other participants at the same time. Slack brings a user’s whole workspace into view, making it easy to follow channels and automate tasks. Salesforce helps teams manage customer relationships and act on business insights, with more of their dashboards in view.

The company goes on to name other apps, including Fantastical, Notewise, Things, Bear, Detail, Instagram, Edits, and VLLO. Apple Arcade games ready for the new form factor include Sneaky Sasquatch and Retrocade.

More apps and sample screenshots are shared in the company’s announcement.

If you’ve already ordered the iPhone Duo or are heading to an Apple store to try one, reviewers recommend trying the inner display in both landscape and portrait modes to see which delivers the better experience. Different third-party apps tend to be optimized for one or the other.

title: Wyze Solar Cam has a 2K camera and needs just an hour of sunlight to keep recording
snippet: Wyze is launching a new Solar Cam that has a camera that matches the best Google Nest has to offer, while needing just an hour of sunlight to avoid needing to manually recharge. more…
fullText:
Wyze is launching a new Solar Cam that has a camera that matches the best Google Nest has to offer, while needing just an hour of sunlight to avoid needing to manually recharge.

Wyze has a camera for basically every need, and its latest is one that works outdoors with potentially limitless battery life. The Wyze Solar Cam bundles a 2K camera with a 1.77W solar panel that Wyze says needs just an hour of direct sunlight to keep charged.

The camera houses a 5,200 mAh battery to ensure it can run in the case of crummy weather or having its solar panel blocked, but in direct sunlight, the panel doesn’t need much to maintain the battery. That’s nothing super new – Wyze itself launched a Solar Cam Pan with the same promise last year, and plenty of other brands have done the same. You can even add a solar panel to a Nest Cam if you really want to.

The benefit of this latest Wyze Solar Cam comes partially in the resolution, with a 2304 x 1296 2K camera that features 130-degree field of view and color night vision. It also has a 100 lumen spotlight built-in and optional local microSD card recording. 

	

Wyze Solar Cam is available today for $69.98, with the camera also available without the solar panel for $10 less.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m reading about an incredible medical plagiarism scandal, replaying the original Ocarina of Time ahead of its remake’s November 5th release, jamming to the dark new Fontaines D.C. album, and using Gemini to prep for the upcoming fantasy basketball season.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Over the course of Friday, it quickly became clear that demand for the iPhone Duo far outstripped initial supply. Apple’s first foldable went on sale at 8am on the 16th, and delivery dates immediately got pushed back to November, then December, and now January. Analysts had warned that Apple wouldn’t be able to keep pace with interest, despite the phone’s $2,000 price, but the company called it “nothing short of extraordinary” in a statement released to the media.

	

Samsung was benefiting before Apple even opened the order books. Its UK mobile leadership says purchases of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 family are up 16% since launch, while Google searches for Samsung foldables rose 300% over the preceding month.

The big question, though, is whether the Duo’s existence will bring the book-style foldable — and by extension, the $2,000 smartphone — into the mainstream. Samsung has been beating this drum since 2019, but foldable share still sits at a mere 2% of the overall smartphone market, and most units sold are the smaller, cheaper flip-style variety. The Duo is expected to give Apple a 25% share of the entire foldable market by the end of 2026, which should broaden acceptance of the form factor across the industry.

I’m not surprised by the uptick in interest; the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is undoubtedly my favorite foldable ever, owing to its novel and pocketable design. I’ve always enjoyed reading on book-style foldables, but with the Fold 8 I often forget I’m using a phone entirely.

Will there be a day when, say,  a decade from now, foldables are the conventional smartphone choice and slab phones of any kind are considered budget alternatives? In a world where component prices stay elevated and companies continue to pad their margins with premium options at the expense of the entry class, that’s a real possibility. Either way, the Duo validates far more than Samsung’s decision to experiment with foldables all those years ago; its unprecedented demand hints at a sea change in how people want to use their phones, and the compromises they’re willing to accept in order to get there.

It’s been a busy week for Samsung news

Samsung just released Android 17 updates for Galaxy S23 and several more devices. Android 17 is a bigger update than one might think, primarily for its improvements to stability and performance.

Samsung’s Android 18-based One UI 10 update sounds like it might be a big deal. One UI 9 is still steaming from the oven, but we’re already dreaming of ways its successor will copy iOS.

I’ve struggled to use Samsung displays for years, but the Galaxy S27 may finally fix that; here’s why

Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating. I don’t think this rumor has legs; Samsung always goes with the best SoC available unless it’s an absolute disaster (see the Snapdragon 810 debacle), and I doubt this one is.

Qualcomm says rumors about Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 overheating are ‘inaccurate’

Samsung reportedly hasn’t finalized Galaxy S27 details, considers February launch. Wouldn’t surprise me if they’re trying to keep costs down.

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Ben Schoon, 9to5Google’s Senior Editor and one of the best disc golf players I know.

Who are you?

Ben Schoon

What do you do for work?

I am the Senior Editor at 9to5Google, covering daily news, reviews, and more.

What do you do for fun?

Disc golf has basically taken over my non-work life. I’ve got a 170-plus-week streak of playing at least once a week, I frequently play in and even run tournaments, and I’m absolutely hooked.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I still deeply enjoy tech, but the AI era has certainly changed my outlook, and not always in the best ways. On the bright side, it’s cool to see the explosion of what tech can do. On the downside, let’s just say that humanity tends to take the path of least resistance, and AI enables that in some frightening ways.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

Nourish has been a huge part of my weight-loss journey over the past couple of years, helping me log food more easily while also connecting with an actual nutritionist. 

UDisc might as well be in my dock row given how frequently I’m out on the disc golf course.

Beeper continues to be indispensable given my multi-device lifestyle.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

The Fitbit Air has been a refreshing bit of simplicity in a busy tech life.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

As mentioned, my relationship with AI isn’t always positive. Lately I find myself more and more frustrated by the impact it’s made on day-to-day life for everyone, and wishing we could go back. Ultimately, I barely find myself using AI in my own life, but I do appreciate those occasional bits of delight that come from finding a good use for it.

What’s a TV show you recently watched and loved?

Recently started listening to the “How We Made Your Mother” podcast and it’s unlocked a fresh rewatch of the early seasons of HIMYM with some new perspectives.

What’s a movie you recently watched and loved?

Project Hail Mary hasn’t left my mind all year. It continues to be a source of joy from its excellent visuals and plot, and the vocal stims that still find their way into daily conversation with my wife and me.

What’s a game you recently played and loved?

Star Wars: Galactic Racer has me hooked right now. I love a good racing game, and this one delivers a real challenge.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spend time around my crazy doggos.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Over the weekend, I caught up on some podcasts and just happened to listen to an episode of The New York Times’ The Daily from a few days ago. “When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life” features an interview with mathematician and Cornell University professor Steven Strogatz, and is among the most poignant and honest conversations I’ve heard about how AI stands to reconfigure everyone’s jobs — even the ones we previously considered unassailable.

There’s recently been an abundance of great reporting on how AI is changing the fields of mathematics and science. But I think some of it lacks the emotional intelligence to acknowledge that LLMs are not just disrupting jobs and preempting discovery; their seemingly infinite potential undermines what it means to be a human solving problems for their own sake. As people become increasingly comfortable offloading their cognition to machines, what happens to their relationship with their own brains?

🗑️ Trash

Anthropic recently announced that it would set aside 5% of its shares to be used for the “public good,” a vacuous claim that has shades of effective altruism. Elon Musk, who is practically single-handedly bankrolling the Republicans’ midterm election, then came out with a similar, more direct offer: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”

The moves are a direct result of a growing public backlash against AI’s negative impacts on culture, on employment, and increasingly on the environment, but laundering one’s reputation with the promise of future beneficence often has the inverse effect.

title: Spotify confirms it won’t stop Family Plan sharing verification, but it’s not a ‘crackdown’
snippet: Earlier this week a new method of Spotify Family plan verification came to light and, in its latest earnings call, Spotify says that it’s not a “crackdown,” but also something that doesn’t have an “end date.” more…
fullText:
Earlier this week a new method of Spotify Family plan verification came to light and, in its latest earnings call, Spotify says that it’s not a “crackdown,” but also something that doesn’t have an “end date.”

Like virtually every family sharing subscription, Spotify requires Family Plan members to be in the same physical household, but the music streaming app has been looser in its requirements and enforcement. A new method, though, started popping up recently in the form of a verification QR code that makes it a bit more difficult for remote participants to complete verification, and also threatens to ban users from Family plans for a full year if verification isn’t completed.

Spotify’s ‘QR code verification’ cracks down on sharing and could ban you for a year

Today, Spotify’s Q3 earnings call included a question about Spotify “beginning to crack down on Family Plan subscribers that do not live in the same home.” 

Responding to this, Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström says that this is not a “crackdown,” but a “routine improvement of our verification methods,” and something that Spotify will continue to work on. “This is not something that has an end date,” he said:

	

…this is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base. As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.

Reading between the lines, this is saying that Spotify isn’t going to be backing down from verification methods on its Family Plan sharing. QR codes are only the latest implementation.

title: Is the Ninja MultiPot the Kitchen Appliance You Need, or Just the One You Want?
snippet: Ninja releases kitchen appliances so often that it’s hard to keep up. Here’s whether or not the new MultiPot XL is a true kitchen essential.
fullText:
When I think of kitchen brands dominating home kitchens and wishlists alike, Ninja immediately comes to mind. 

Beyond the company’s viral social media videos and massively popular product releases, like the Crispi air fryer and Creami frozen dessert maker, the brand’s popularity may also be rooted in its rapid product launches. Ninja releases products fast, and it releases a lot of them. 

In the last couple of months alone, we’ve seen the release of the Prepi, CrushBoss, NeverQuit cookware and now, the MultiPot XL. With colder weather setting in, the 12-in-1 cooker caught my eye. Theoretically, it can reduce kitchen clutter by replacing numerous other countertop appliances, but is it truly a worthy replacement for your Instant Pot, Crockpot and even the classic Dutch oven? 

		

			

With so many new releases, how do you separate want from need? We cooked numerous meals with the new MultiPot XL to see whether the shiny new appliance has what it takes to earn a place on your countertop. 

Searing, sautéing and soups 

The MultiPot XL has 12 settings: Slow cook, sear/sauté, bake, steam, sous vide, rice, pasta, mixed rice, stir fry, shallow fry, hot pot and keep warm.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

The Ninja MultiPot XL has 12 functions and the option to cook in the “Megazone,” a 7.5-quart pot, or in two smaller pots, each 3.5 quarts. All of the pots are ceramic-coated. 

The first meal I cooked in it was homemade ramen, and I learned there are a few settings where the MultiPot excels, including the sear/sauté function. 

The first ingredient I sautéed was mushrooms with butter. The MultiPot quickly preheated and sauteed the mushrooms just as well as a non-stick pan on a stovetop would. When the lids are shut, the pot quickly gathers steam to help speed up the cooking process too. 

Next, I placed the chicken thighs in the already heated pot, and they took only a few minutes to cook all the way through. The best part was that the chicken developed a crust, which added extra flavor to the dish. 

I used the same function for a handful of additional ingredients, combined everything in the pot with chicken broth and then set the MultiPot to its hot pot setting until everything came to a boil.  

Because the pot was already hot, it didn’t take long to boil. When I was ready for it to stop, I turned off the appliance and lifted the pot off the hot plates so it wouldn’t overcook. Over the next couple of weeks, I continued to use the appliance for various meals, but sauté/sear and hot pot remained among my favorite functions.  

A loaded vegetable soup was one of my favorite meals I made. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

It’s not a slow cooker replacement

Despite its ability to sear and sauté just as well as a non-stick pan on the stovetop, one setting was less impressive. I used the slow cooker setting to cook a small batch of beef short ribs in one half of the cooker, cooking them on low for over 8 hours. I’ve cooked this meal before in a slow cooker, and by the end of the 8 hours, the meat is usually falling apart and my whole house smells like the dish. 

With the MultiPot, though, although the meat was still fully cooked through and had a great flavor, it wasn’t fall-off-the-bone cooked. I’m not entirely sure why that is, but it made me wish I’d cooked that dish in my Crockpot instead. 

Being able to cook two things at once on different settings is a high point for the appliance. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

On the other side of the MultiPot, I cooked brown rice, and it cooked just as well as on the stovetop.

In my experience, the only place where the MultiPot has a leg up on a slow cooker is the fact that you can sauté or sear directly in the MultiPot, then turn the pot to the slow cooker setting, instead of having to sear in a separate pan on the stovetop, then transfer the ingredients to a slow cooker. So, if you’re looking for convenience, the MultiPot offers it. 

I was also able to thicken up my short rib sauce directly in the pot on the sear/sauté setting instead of transferring it to the stovetop. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

Who’s the Ninja MultiPot XL best for? 

If you have limited countertop space for appliances and want just one that can handle many cooking tasks, the MultiPot XL would be a great option. With 12 settings, it has more versatility than many competitors, but keep in mind that the “keep warm” function is included in the 12, and some functions won’t be used as much as others, such as sous vide. 

At $250, it’s more expensive than standard slow cookers and Instant Pots, but it could be a good option if you often cook large meals for a group. If you’re looking for a cheaper multicooker, but want to stay in the Ninja family, the 8-in-1 Ninja PossibleCooker may be a smarter buy since it’s less than half the price but still has the essential functions. However, I haven’t tested the PossibleCooker myself.

The MultiPot XL can definitely be a great choice for some, but I wouldn’t put it in the must-have category, even if the rose quartz option is one of the cutest appliance color schemes I’ve seen.
