title: Beyond the Review: Inside the Onyx RCR 80V E-Bike
snippet: The Onyx RCR 80V can hit motorcycle speeds, but after hundreds of miles in the saddle, I found there’s a lot more to this compact e-bike than going fast.
fullText:
The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York, I’m more interested in what this electric bike is like to live with.

The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?

My impression is that Onyx is trying to build a compact electric motorbike with BMX-inspired maneuverability and modern electronics, while leaving owners room to customize it and keep it running. Riding the RCR and talking with Onyx founder Tim Seward helped me understand that approach. Whether it holds up over years of ownership is a question a few hundred miles can’t answer.

			

More from CNET

Joseph Kaminski

Onyx RCR 80V GeekBox

Manufacturer figures below are advertised specifications, not independently measured performance results. Prices as of Oct. 14.

Specification

Onyx RCR 80V

Starting price

$4,699 Street / $4,899 Dual Sport

Motor

Rear hub; advertised 8kW nominal

Battery

Removable 80V, 45Ah / 3.6kWh

Claimed top speed

65–75 mph, depending on configuration; advertised for off-road use

Claimed maximum range

140 miles; current table associates this with Cruise Tune Eco at 15 mph

Claimed acceleration

0–30 mph in 1.7 seconds

Ride modes tested

Eco, Normal, Sport and Hyper

Wheels

17-inch tubeless

Brakes

Hydraulic discs with 220mm rotors

Display

TFT touchscreen

Phone integration

Apple CarPlay / Android Auto

Other features

Reverse, cruise control, regenerative braking, turn signals and alarm/key fob

Advertised ready-to-ride weight

Approximately 155 pounds

Sources: Onyx model and pricing overview⁠, RCR product page⁠, RCR feature page⁠ and Onyx’s brake and wheel description⁠.

Joseph Maldonado

Street, Dual Sport and getting it home

The Street and Dual Sport share the advertised motor and battery ratings. Their clearest hardware differences are the tires and fenders: Street has 4-inch street tires with optional fenders; Dual Sport has 4.5-inch tires with a more aggressive tread and fenders included. (See how the models compare at Onyx.⁠)

Neither arrives like a lightweight bicycle. The RCR is a heavy freight delivery that still needs final assembly, and I wouldn’t recommend unpacking it alone. At roughly 155 pounds ready to ride, it also demands some thought about storage before you order.

I live in a three-flight walk-up. That matters more to my daily experience than another few miles per hour at the top end.

Yes, the RCR has pedals. I doubt many people are spending nearly $5,000 because they’re looking forward to using them.

Joseph Maldonado

Small bike, serious performance

I’m 6 feet tall, around 260 pounds and usually carrying a backpack. The RCR has had no trouble moving me around.

Most of my riding has been between 15 and 35 mph, with plenty of time in Normal. I haven’t often felt the need for more. What I appreciate is the reserve power for acceleration and hills, rather than having to ask the bike for everything just to carry a heavier rider.

Seward made a similar point when we talked about the RCR’s development around San Francisco. Steep hills help explain why usable power matters beyond a top-speed claim.

His background also helps explain the bike. An industrial designer whose portfolio includes projects for Sonos and Bird, Seward founded Onyx to bring classic motorbike character to an electric machine. ⁠

He described a combination of motorcycle performance and BMX-style maneuverability. I grew up racing BMX, and I can relate to that influence. The RCR’s compact dimensions make it easy to move around underneath me and maneuver in tighter spaces. Its size is part of its appeal, although the weight is a reminder that this is a very different machine from a BMX bike.

“It’s like a blank canvas that you can customize… It’s not a BMX at all, but it definitely has some influence from when I was a kid,” says Seward.

Joseph Maldonado

The throttle changes the experience

With this much power, how it arrives matters.

On my test bike, Eco and Normal feel smoother and more forgiving. Sport and Hyper respond more immediately to wrist movement. Switching modes changes more than the available speed; it changes how carefully I need to feed in the throttle.

I like having that choice. Sometimes I want an easy cruise. Other times, I appreciate a quicker response. A gentler mode doesn’t eliminate the need for careful throttle control, but it makes the bike’s delivery better suited to how I want to ride.

These impressions apply to the software on my test bike. They aren’t a comparison of Onyx’s newer Cruise and Thrill tunes.

What I can say about range

I haven’t completed a controlled range test, so I don’t have a measured full-charge figure to give you.

What I do have is several hundred miles of use without range anxiety. On one ride from around 151st Street in Harlem to East 26th Street, the display showed a drop of about nine percentage points. My ride took me through Central Park, so we’re looking at about 9 miles. After longer outings through Queens and Brooklyn, I’ve returned with roughly 60% to 70% of the indicated charge remaining.

My much lighter teenage son also rode the RCR on an outing through those boroughs. I recall the indicated charge dropping by 17%, although that wasn’t a controlled comparison with my own riding.

One thing that continues to impress me about the Onyx RCR 80V is just how quiet its motor is. There’s none of that high-pitched whining or wheezing you sometimes hear from electric motors. Power delivery is equally impressive, remaining smooth and consistent whether I’m accelerating from a standstill or riding at higher speeds. I’ve also noticed how much the route itself can affect battery consumption. On a recent commute from 151st Street to East 26th Street, I took a different route instead of traveling entirely through Central Park and used just 6% of the battery compared with 9% on a previous ride. It’s a good reminder that real-world range isn’t simply about distance. Terrain, elevation changes, traffic, speed and riding conditions all influence how efficiently the bike uses energy.

Joseph Maldonado

Those readings describe what I saw on the display. They don’t establish that each percentage point equals a mile, or that the bike will travel 100 miles on a charge. Without recorded distances, consistent conditions and a fuller discharge test, that would be an extrapolation.

Rider weight, speed, acceleration and terrain all matter. My conclusion is narrower: the battery has comfortably covered the rides I’ve taken. Someone spending more time at high speed should expect a different experience.

Onyx itself recommends watching battery voltage for a better indication of remaining charge and range. That’s another reason to treat my percentage readings as observations rather than precision measurements. (Here’s Onyx’s battery guidance.⁠)

Joseph Maldonado

Comfortable suspension, with limits at the seat

The RCR fits me surprisingly well, and the suspension has done a good job taking the edge off New York’s potholes and broken pavement.

The seat is comfortable with good cushioning for shorter rides. After about 90 minutes, though, I start shifting around. The suspension helps with the road underneath me, but it doesn’t eliminate the discomfort that builds during a longer ride. That also could be due to my size; I’m far from a lightweight. 

The brakes have also felt consistently strong. After a few hundred miles, lever travel still feels close to how it did at the start, and I haven’t noticed a meaningful decline in stopping performance. That’s a riding impression, not a measured stopping-distance or brake-wear test.

Cruise control and reverse were pleasant surprises

Cruise control sounded like a minor convenience until I used it. On the inclines I’ve encountered with it engaged, the RCR has held the selected speed even with my weight aboard. That has been a more useful demonstration of its available power than a top-speed run.

Discovering that it could also reverse was another pleasant surprise. On a machine this heavy, powered reverse is a feature I’m glad to have. Onyx documents both functions in its advanced controls guide.

Joseph Maldonado

CarPlay is a favorite feature — and a frustration

I didn’t expect to care this much about CarPlay. Having navigation and audio controls on the built-in display means I can leave my phone put away.

My main complaint is what happens to the motorbike’s own information. While using CarPlay, especially during a call, I want speed and battery status to remain easy to see. On my test bike, they aren’t presented as conveniently as I’d like.

Onyx told me it intends to address the display issue through a software update.

Navigation brings up another issue. I’d like routing that better reflects the vehicle I’m riding. Because it uses CarPlay, it offers driving directions. However, I would like the option to choose a different route if I choose to.

“Having Android Auto and CarPlay in the bike makes me want to ride more … Part of the new update will show stats like battery level and mode on the side while using it,” says Seward, who is also Onyx’s chief design officer.

Joseph Maldonado

Signals, lights and wet pavement

The turn signals sit close to the body, with less protruding hardware to catch on something. I like that design, but in sunny settings, the signals may not be as visible.

They don’t self-cancel. The display indicators help, but I’d prefer automatic cancellation to discovering I’ve announced a left turn for the last 20 blocks (a minor complaint). The Bluetooth connection indicator is another small, useful display detail.

The headlight has worked well for the nighttime riding I’ve done. The halo running light and main beam give the bike a distinctive look, with high beam available when needed.

Joseph Maldonado

I’ve also ridden in the rain and on wet pavement without noticing handling problems. That’s limited experience, not a comprehensive wet-weather test. The more immediate issue is spray, as my bike doesn’t have the optional fenders installed, and New York street water gets everywhere.

Fenders are high on my list before doing more wet-weather riding.

Tubeless tires and everyday maintenance

The tubeless setup matters to me because removing a motorized rear wheel to deal with a flat tube can become a project. I’d rather avoid that extra complication where possible.

Tubeless doesn’t mean puncture-proof, and I wouldn’t assume any roadside plug is a permanent repair suitable for motorcycle speeds. But it’s a great go-to when in a pinch. Not having to remove the wheel to make it to your destination is clutch. 

“These are basically motorcycle wheels and tires, so if you get a nail, you can patch or plug it without taking the wheel off and replacing the whole tube,” says Seward.

Joseph Kaminski

Forget the fob and the bike stays put

I’ve kept the RCR in storage at my partner’s apartment because she has an elevator. I sometimes forget to leave the key fob with it, which works well until I arrive without the fob.

That experience made phone or NFC access more appealing. Seward told me Onyx is developing app-based diagnostics, firmware updates and service support, and we discussed possible phone access. I’d welcome it, along with integrated tracking or movement alerts.

For now, I keep an AirTag hidden in the bike. I’ve also found the rear-wheel locking behavior reassuring when the bike is secured, although that isn’t a substitute for a physical lock.

Onyx already links a Superpower BMS app for battery monitoring. That should be distinguished from the broader app and unlocking features we discussed; I haven’t established that those proposed functions are available. (See the Onyx product page.)

Joseph Maldonado

The pedals don’t settle the legal question

I think of the RCR as a compact electric motorcycle. That description doesn’t, by itself, establish whether a particular example can be registered for road use. But it can be insured.

New York’s legal definition of an electric-assist bicycle includes a motor below 750 watts and specified assistance-speed limits. The RCR’s advertised power and performance exceed those limits. Buyers shouldn’t assume that pedals or a lower-speed setting make it a legal e-bike. (See New York’s DMV definitions.)⁠

I haven’t verified New York registration eligibility for this exact model and configuration. That needs to be resolved with the DMV and the manufacturer before it can be presented as a straightforward street-legal commuting option. Bicycle lanes and walking routes should not be assumed available to it.

Joseph Maldonado

Beyond the ride: A conversation with Tim Seward

Seward’s explanation of Onyx starts with the products he no longer wanted to design. During our conversation, he described working on consumer electronics for brands including Sonos, HP and Samsung, only to watch products become disposable shortly after reaching the market. His experiences with furniture and old gas-powered mopeds suggested a different approach.

The following excerpts are edited for length and clarity from the interview transcript. Questions have been shortened, and the discussion has been reordered by topic. Future features are plans described during the interview, not confirmation that they are available today.

Joseph Maldonado

CNET: Is there anything about your background or the bike that people might not know?

Seward: Before Onyx, I was a big consumer-electronics designer. I worked on Sonos, HP, Samsung, and all sorts of products you would see at Best Buy. While I liked that job, I didn’t like that people were throwing away their products.

When I was customizing gas-powered mopeds, I realized I was working on vehicles 30 to 50 years old. Who knows how many hands it went through until it got to me? I was like, I need to make products like this. I need to make products that, even if Onyx dies tomorrow, the products will live on. I didn’t want to continue to create landfill.

Joseph Maldonado

If an owner keeps this bike for five years, what can they realistically expect for battery health?

With our extra layer of health protections, we are confident our battery pack will show only a 10% degradation in 10 years. So, at the five-year mark, you won’t even notice much of a difference, if any, in performance.

(That’s an ambitious prediction. Seward’s response didn’t include the testing, charging habits or usage conditions behind it, so I wouldn’t treat it as a guaranteed outcome or a warranty. It does give me something specific to follow up on as the bike ages.)

How committed is Onyx to supporting owners with replacement parts years down the road?

We strive to offer hard-to-find parts even for discontinued products that are 5 to 6 years old. Also, our newest model, the RCR 80V, uses many parts that are compatible with aftermarket upgrades, so you can modify or maintain it for decades to come.

(That gets to one of my biggest questions about an expensive electric vehicle: What happens when something breaks after the model is no longer current? Aftermarket compatibility could help keep the RCR running, although it isn’t a guarantee that every component will remain available.)

Joseph Maldonado

What sets Onyx apart from the growing number of electric motorcycle companies?

We are not just building a bike. We are building a community of riders who support each other across the globe.

(That connects with how I found my way to Onyx. I met John Angel while testing another bike, and he kept encouraging me to try an RCR. Before I spoke with the company, another rider had already shared his experience and got me interested.

The community side matters most when it becomes useful: Someone helping you understand a feature, troubleshoot a problem or figure out a modification. That’s the kind of owner involvement I’d like to see continue as Onyx grows.

Onyx also brings its community together through events like Onyx Week, where owners and enthusiasts participate in organized rides, meet members of the Onyx team, exchange ideas, and connect with other riders. Events have been organized in Los Angeles and New York, giving owners an opportunity to experience the community beyond online discussions and social media.)

Joseph Maldonado

What stays with me

The RCR has more power than I usually need and has covered my outings without battery anxiety. CarPlay and cruise control have become features I actually value. The seat can become less comfortable on longer rides, and the display should show the current speed and battery level while on a call. 

Talking with Seward gave me a clearer understanding of the decisions behind those experiences. Customer feedback helped shape the 80V, while his experience with disposable electronics explains why he wants owners to keep these bikes running.

Joseph Maldonado

It’s nice to hear a company talk about making something you can keep for years instead of pushing you to buy a new model every year. That intention still has to be backed by replacement parts, documentation and service. Onyx’s published guidance says it doesn’t repair, refurbish or rebalance batteries, so long-term battery support remains an important question. (See Onyx’s battery support policy.)⁠

For me, that’s what makes this worth looking at beyond the review — understanding why the RCR was built this way, how owners influence what comes next and whether the support can live up to the design. Would I recommend getting one? Heck yeah!

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Joseph Kaminski
						

						

							Senior Associate Technology Editor / Reviews						
					

											

								

											During my almost twenty years at CNET, I handled benchmark testing/methodologies for both Mac and PC systems and, sometime after, integrated testing for micro-mobility (e-bikes, electric scooters and EUCs), which is a passion of mine. Transitioning from a BMX background to this field was seamless. 
Despite testing numerous products, each new one brings the same excitement as my first.
															
						See full bio
excerpt:
The first thing people ask about the Onyx RCR 80V is how fast it goes. After hundreds of miles around New York, I’m more interested in what this electric bike is like to live with.

The acceleration certainly gets your attention. But so do the compact proportions, CarPlay, cruise control and little design decisions that become more noticeable the longer you ride. Then there are the bigger questions: Can you repair it? Will parts still be available? What happens when the technology gets old?

title: Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports [U]
snippet: After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports. more…
fullText:
After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports.

On the homepage, you’ll see a notification bell icon next to the profile switcher in the top-right corner. Tapping opens a feed with “updates about items in Wallet.” 

Earlier this month, the company said it was introducing an “in-app message center in Google Wallet.” This new feature is still rolling out via a server-side update.

Meanwhile, Google Wallet is adding support for more digital passports. Officially referred to as an “ID pass” in the app, usage varies by country. US passports can be used at TSA security via NFC or QR code scanning. 

	

Update 10/23: Following Brazil, Singapore, Taiwan, United Kingdom, and the United States of America, we’re starting to see the ability to add Estonia, Ireland, Italy, and Spain.

The new countries are not widely rolled out yet.

To add a passport, tap the ‘plus’ FAB at the bottom of Google Wallet > IDs & personal info > ID pass. The registration process involves scanning your passport info page and security chip. Afterward, you have to record a video of your face. You’ll get a notification once verification is complete.

title: Android has always been chaotic in the best ways possible
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

The through-line in every iPhone Duo review yesterday was this: excellent hardware (though a bit too heavy) and a chaotic software experience. When Apple’s foldable launches on Friday, it will remind early adopters of what Android used to feel like whenever a new form factor was introduced: exciting, janky, and slightly aggravating.

	

I think 9to5Google readers understand that Android is for tweakers. It’s why so many of you sign up for Android betas on daily-driver hardware; it’s why there’s a thriving community of indie developers filling gaps in the ecosystem. Android’s freedom and flexibility (and cost) make it particularly well suited to the cavalcade of use cases and designs we see in the market today.

That openness confers other, more nebulous benefits; it’s far easier to emulate games on Android along with other legally grey activities that won’t be mentioned here. If there’s something you want to do on Android, chances are you can figure out a way to do it.

It seems like the iPhone Duo’s early adopters will be faced with a similar conundrum: the ability to do more on a device that is likely to frustrate and delight in equal measure. As Ben explains in his iPhone Duo review roundup, “the app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet.”

But as with all things iPhone, app and software improvements are likely to come quickly and consistently over the next few months and years. Ben eloquently sums up the situation: “Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start.”

✉️ Inbox

Galaxy S27 might drop to 8GB of RAM; other Android phones could go back to 4GB. Not sure I entirely believe this rumor, but it is true that Google has been making Android more memory-efficient, so maybe it is true?

ModRetro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it? This product feels like the physical manifestation of using X.

Spotify podcast memberships let you support your favorite shows and get added perks. I support this feature, but the continued fragmentation of the podcast subscription ecosystem is driving me crazy.

Iron Man himself now officially endorses Snap’s latest smart glasses. Because he’s the only person who can afford to buy them.

Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji. Depending on who you ask, this is a good thing or a terrible thing.

Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer. Perfect timing with yesterday’s PHP vulnerabilities.

You can cut your cell phone bill to $10/month or get a Pixel 11 for $400 right now – here’s how. Some decent deals from Mint Mobile (#notsponsored).

YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos. This makes sense to me; dislike buttons used to be there to help shape your algorithm, but there are so many other ways to do that today that its existence feels unnecessary.

Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence. I can’t wait to ask Gemini about that mole on my back while driving my in-laws around the city.

Google Maps on CarPlay rolling out Gemini when navigating

Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 for Pixel rolling out with 21 fixes. (Almost) nothing to see here.

Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 [Gallery]

Google rolling out minor Nest Hub update

Samsung is rolling out Android 17 updates for some of its most popular Galaxy phones

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Google gives Pixel 9 another year of free Satellite SOS connectivity. I have a feeling this isn’t the last announcement of this kind we’ll see.

Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you

The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say. This has been a very good year for book-style foldables, and the momentum is slated to continue into 2027.

Google reiterates missing Fitbit Air sleep breathing quality feature coming ‘soon’

Google TV powers the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro glasses, and that’s exactly the problem

Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports

OpenAI GPT models are coming to Google Antigravity ‘soon,’ Cloud ‘in the coming weeks’. OpenAI and Microsoft continue their very public divorce.

Xbox Cloud Gaming’s added playtime costs start at around 40¢ per hour. Who is asking for this feature?

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music. The app may be an iOS clone, but I’m happy it exists.

Non-folding phones can still be interesting

Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price

The real reason to care about Vivo’s latest phone is the camera [Gallery]

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

I was the guest on this week’s Sideload episode, and we talked about my favorite thing: AI. In particular, how we use AI in our daily lives.

One thing we touched on that I’m going to delve into in a future newsletter is whether Google is actually behind the competition with Gemini. With the recent release of Gemini 4 Argon, it’s clear the company is close to the frontier, but the more important question to answer is whether Gemini is a good product. I make the argument that it is, especially because Google has its tendrils in every part of my life, from email to search to maps, and that makes Gemini’s answers far more useful when I ask it questions of a personal nature. That it has a 25% market share right now is almost accidental; so many people are forced to interact with Gemini in one way or another through Google’s various products.

It’s also bizarre that Google hasn’t figured out a way to compete with Meta on the personal agent front. On its earnings call, Meta said that Muse has been used by over 10 million people, and 25% of them use it every day. Google has Spark, but it’s not in the same league in terms of functionality or mindshare.

Google is unquestionably behind Anthropic and OpenAI where the money is made: in the enterprise. Antigravity is a subpar harness, and Argon is a capable but unspectacular coding agent.

Nevertheless, Google has the money, the user base, and, most importantly, the incentive to keep going after the top labs. In an interview this week with Alex Kantrowitz, CEO Sundar Pichai said that he is committed to the frontier at all costs, and that Google Cloud compute capacity is being reallocated in 2027 to train state-of-the-art models.

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s proactive AI agent answer to Muse and OpenAI’s Dots

It’s almost Thanksgiving travel season, which means it’s time to re-up one of the best Onion videos about the places our souls go to die: airports.

As mentioned above, Supernatural is relaunching on the Quest as a new independent app with the original owners and much of the same crew. When Meta announced that it was laying off much of its Reality Labs division and shutting Supernatural down, it didn’t look good for the future of what I consider the best VR workout app ever made. But by the summer, it was announced that Meta had negotiated a sale of the brand and IP (but not the code), which allowed the formation of Supernatural Health.

Launching this week in Early Access, it’s now double what it used to cost — $200 a year — but it’s one of the few subscriptions I look forward to paying. If you’re a Quest owner, I cannot recommend it highly enough.

✍️ Signature

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Tuesday.

-Daniel

title: Google Health 5.11 rolling out expanded 100+ activity detection to Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch
snippet: With the Fitbit Edge announcement, Google Health previewed improved automatic activity tracking, and it’s now beginning to roll out with version 5.11 of the app. more…
fullText:
With the Fitbit Edge announcement, Google Health previewed improved automatic activity tracking, and it’s now beginning to roll out with version 5.11 of the app.

This expanded activity tracking means the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 go from detecting 10 activities to more than 100, including:

Cardio machines

Golf

High-intensity workouts

Racket sports

Strength training

Swimming

Team sports

The Fitbit Edge will also benefit from this upgrade. Google Health pairs your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and location (permission required) with contextual reasoning.

Workouts that result in a sustained elevated heart rate and meet the minimum duration threshold are automatically logged, with a summary notification sent to the app “typically within 30 minutes.” When you “confirm or edit an activity” and log missing ones, Google will learn your patterns to tune future predictions.

	

Google says the end result is “nearly 2x more accurate detections,” while reducing “missed workouts by more than half.”

Expanded activity detection is appearing with Google Health 5.11, which is widely available on iOS and still rolling out on Android. After updating, users are seeing an “Expanded activity detection, built to learn” screen.

title: Apple and DOJ notify court of impasse over document cutoff in antitrust lawsuit
snippet: Apple and the Department of Justice have submitted a joint notice of impasse over how recent Apple’s documents must be to fall within the scope of discovery in their ongoing antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and the Department of Justice have submitted a joint notice of impasse over how recent Apple’s documents must be to fall within the scope of discovery in their ongoing antitrust lawsuit. Here are the details.

A bit of context

In March 2024, the Department of Justice, alongside 15 states and the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of illegally maintaining a monopoly in the smartphone market.

In essence, they accuse Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case. Interestingly, Apple and the DOJ have also reportedly been engaged in settlement talks behind the scenes.

Back to the disputes, they have included how many Apple employees’ records should be searched, whether Apple must produce documents from outside the US, and Apple’s efforts to obtain records from 14 federal agencies, which the government continues to challenge.

Amid these disputes, the discovery schedule has been extended several times, which brings us to today’s filing.

Apple and DOJ at odds over document production cutoff

In a joint notice filed today, Apple and the DOJ inform the court of “an impasse concerning

the cutoff date for Apple’s productions in response to all Requests for Production.”

According to the DOJ, while the two sides initially agreed to a June 20, 2025 cutoff for the documents Apple would be required to produce, that date was based on the original discovery schedule, which has since been pushed back.

In practical terms, the June 20, 2025 cutoff date was agreed upon with the expectation that fact discovery would be completed by July 31, 2026. However, that deadline has since been extended twice, and is now scheduled for late May 2027.

As a result, the DOJ argues that Apple should be required to update its document production to include records created up to 30 days before fact discovery closes, warning that sticking to the original cutoff could prevent the government from obtaining evidence of Apple’s allegedly “ongoing anticompetitive conduct.”

Plaintiffs contend they should not be prejudiced in obtaining and presenting evidence of Apple’s ongoing anticompetitive conduct by the extended fact discovery schedule, particularly when Apple requested the delay. Plaintiffs believe that Apple’s proposal to consider supplementation on a case-by-case basis is unworkable, likely to generate more disputes over the course of fact discovery, and inconsistent with Apple’s duty to supplement under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(e).

Apple, on the other hand, argues that the June 2025 cutoff was part of a negotiated agreement and that the DOJ’s request would effectively restart the document discovery process, introducing “months of delay into this case.”

The parties previously agreed to a presumptive June 20, 2025 discovery cut-off. Apple then substantially completed its document productions in the Government Action in 12 months — with a massive investment of resources and hundreds of contractors dedicated to the process. Re-collecting from 54 custodians and numerous other sources, then searching, reviewing, and producing new materials for a 22-month period would take Apple several more months. It is simply not feasible for Apple to produce documents up until 30 days before the close of fact discovery, as that would mean new collections, searches, review, and production within those last 30 days, after almost all depositions will be complete.”

Instead, Apple says it is willing to consider targeted requests for additional documents on a case-by-case basis, an approach the DOJ argues would be unworkable and likely lead to further disputes.

Apple also disputed the DOJ’s suggestion that the company was solely responsible for the schedule extensions and pointed out that the government has yet to produce documents in response to most of Apple’s requests, which were “served over 15 months ago.”

title: Apple still makes it too hard for Apple Pay competitors to emerge, says UK
snippet: Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay … more…
fullText:
Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay …

When Apple first started embedding an NFC chip in iPhones to enable contactless payment, only the Apple Wallet app could take advantage of this. Third-party apps could use the NFC chip for other purposes, but not for card payments.

That saw the iPhone maker facing antitrust action in multiple countries around the world. In a number of them, it’s been forced to unlock access to the chip, most notably in the EU.

In EU countries, developers can request an entitlement to get access by proving to Apple that they meet the industry standards and hold the licenses needed to process consumer payments. No fees are payable. Users are then allowed to choose the default wallet app that appears when they double-click the side button or hold their phone near a payment terminal. 

In the UK, however, the CMA told Reuters that Apple hasn’t offered developers the same terms. 

CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said […] “We have ​heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.”

	

Accordingly, the regulator has opened a public consultation on its proposed loosening of Apple’s grip on the contactless payment chip. Apple has responded by rejecting the proposal, but saying that it will continue to work with the CMA.

“We do ⁠not ​believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an ​approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome ​that is in the best interest of our users.”

9to5Mac’s Take

I see this very much like third-party app stores. While I understand Apple’s position, the company is ultimately likely to lose these battles and is showing no sign of skating to where the regulatory puck is headed.

It seems a needless battle given that the commercial risk to Apple is very limited – the vast majority of iPhone owners are exceedingly unlikely to change the defaults for either app store or wallet app when given the choice.

title: MacBook Neo helps Apple soften the blow of global PC market downturn, per report
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report on global PC shipments for Q3 2026 shows Apple outperforming the broader market, with the MacBook Neo helping cushion the impact of declining demand. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report on global PC shipments for Q3 2026 shows Apple outperforming the broader market, with the MacBook Neo helping cushion the impact of declining demand. Here are the details.

In a new report released today, Counterpoint Research says global PC shipments plunged 21% during Q3 2026, compared with the year-ago period.

In absolute numbers, Counterpoint says global shipments totaled 57 million units, with Lenovo leading the market with a 26.3% share, despite a 23% year-over-year decline.

HP held second place with an 18.1% share and a 31% decline in shipments, followed by Dell (13.3% share, down 25%), Apple (9.8% share, down 11%), and ASUS, which rounded out the top five with a 9.2% share and a 7% decline. Other vendors accounted for the remaining 23.3% of the market, with shipments down 16% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for the quarter:

“Apple’s shipments declined 11% YoY to 5.6 million units, giving it a 9.8% market share, up from 8.7% a year earlier. The MacBook Neo helped cushion the decline, allowing Apple to outperform the overall market.”

Commenting on the results, Counterpoint Research senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that Apple and ASUS outperformed the broader market “through differentiated product portfolios and competitive positioning.”

As most 9to5Mac readers are probably guessing by now, rising memory and other component costs were major contributors to the market-wide downturn. Counterpoint says higher PC prices discouraged consumers from upgrading their devices and weakened demand across the industry.

According to Counterpoint’s data, contract prices for 8GB DDR4 RAM modules rose 24% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, while 1TB NVMe SSD prices increased 29%.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects RAM prices to rise another 13% in Q4 and 15% in Q1 2027, while SSD prices are projected to increase 11% in Q4 before stabilizing in early 2027.

fullText:
iOS 27.2 is coming next week and brings two new features for Apple TV subscribers. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Profiles come to iPhone and iPad, and with new characters

Apple TV is currently the only major streaming service that doesn’t offer user profiles on iPhone and iPad. But that’s about to change with iOS and iPadOS 27.2.

Profiles already exist in tvOS for big-screen viewing of Apple TV content, but now they’re coming to Apple’s other platforms too.

When you create user profiles on one platform, they automatically sync to others, letting you keep playback history, queues, and recommendations all personalized for each viewer. And if you set up a profile for your child, they’ll only see age-appropriate Apple TV content.

Alongside the expansion of profiles to more platforms, Apple has added a variety of new profile image options in iOS 27.2. Characters from Apple TV kids’ series like The Snoopy Show, Frog and Toad, and Stillwater are all now available. 

#2: Sign language support

Apple TV is taking accessibility a step beyond subtitle options by adding official support for sign language on select movies and shows.

With iOS 27.2, users can optionally enable American Sign Language (ASL) or British Sign Language (BSL).

You’ll find the option to enable sign language inside the Settings app under Apps ⇾ TV ⇾ Sign Language. It’s unknown how many Apple TV titles will support sign language initially, but it’s great to see the feature added.

title: Fitbit Edge doesn’t have Google Wallet because ‘less than 1%’ of Charge owners used it
snippet: Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature. more…
fullText:
Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature.

The ability to pay at the register with your wearable is nothing new, but NFC support on smartwatches and trackers has been pretty hit or miss in the past. Google supports the feature as a standard across the Pixel Watch lineup, and the last-gen Fitbit Charge 6 also supported the feature.

But, with the new Fitbit Edge, NFC support is gone and, in turn, so is Google Wallet.

It’s an interesting regression on Google’s part, so why the change? In a statement to Android Authority, Google explains that it really just comes down to a lack of people actually using this feature on the Fitbit Charge 6. 

	

Fitbit Edge does not offer NFC for payments. It was not widely used by our Charge 6 users — in fact, less than 1% reported using the feature on Charge 6 — so we prioritized other top features such as adding an altimeter and requested improvements.

Google says that skipping NFC left room to “prioritize” other features such as the Edge’s new altimeter, but it still seems like a shame to skip out on mobile payments for what is very much a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

	

Would you have used Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge? Is it a dealbreaker? Let us know in the comments below.

Early customers are going to have to contend with third-party apps not yet optimized for the device, but Apple says the situation is improving rapidly as developers get on board. The first reviews based on a week of usage present a consistent view, with app support one of five key takeouts.

title: WhatsApp may soon let iPhone users open any link in an in-app browser
snippet: After introducing limited in-app browser support for certain business links last year, WhatsApp is now working on expanding the feature to all links shared in chats. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After introducing limited in-app browser support for certain business links last year, WhatsApp is now working on expanding the feature to all links shared in chats. Here are the details.

WhatsApp working on optional in-app browser

Last May, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp had begun testing a feature that would allow “users to view certain HTTPS-secured business sites within the app,” with the option to open those links in their default browser via the three-dot menu.

Now, the site reports that WhatsApp is working on extending this support to all in-chat links.

Although the feature is not yet available to beta testers, WABetaInfo has uncovered references to it in the latest TestFlight build and shared screenshots showing how it will work.

According to the site, a new “In-app browser” option under Settings > Chats will let users choose whether links open directly within WhatsApp or in their default browser.

Image: WABetaInfo

The same settings screen will also let users clear cookies, cache, and other browsing data stored by WhatsApp’s in-app browser.

	

Here’s WABetaInfo:

Users will be able to enable the in-app browser from the app settings. Here, WhatsApp will add a new option called “In-app browser”. When users enable this feature, they will be able to open any link they send and receive in the chat screen. When users enable this option for the first time, WhatsApp will show a bottom sheet that explains how the feature works. It informs users that they can now open any link within WhatsApp rather than in the default browser. Users will be able to restore the default browser at any time.

The report notes that “WhatsApp cannot see links shared in the conversation and which ones users open.”

As is usually the case with references discovered in WhatsApp’s TestFlight builds, there is currently no word on when the app plans to make the feature available to beta testers or the general public.

title: Gurman: iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with Face ID are already being tested inside Apple
snippet: The iPhone Duo comes out tomorrow but, given the strong pre-order demand, it is already looking to be a smash hit. And we are all expecting Apple to follow up with a second-generation model next fall, which means the company has to be already working on the next-gen hardware. On his Power On podcast, Mark Gurman reports that iPhone Duo 2 prototypes inside Apple include Face ID, with the Face ID sensor being integrated beneath the display on the outer screen. more…
fullText:
The iPhone Duo comes out tomorrow but, given the strong pre-order demand, it is already looking to be a smash hit. And we are all expecting Apple to follow up with a second-generation model next fall, which means the company has to be already working on the next-gen hardware.

On his Power On podcast, Mark Gurman reports that iPhone Duo 2 prototypes inside Apple include Face ID, with the Face ID sensor being integrated beneath the display on the outer screen.

The shift from Face ID to Touch ID on this phone was one of the biggest complaints raised by early iPhone Duo reviewers. 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller called it “the hardest thing to get used to” with the new foldable.

For the first-gen iPhone Duo, fitting Face ID inside the super-thin enclosure seemed to be the blocker. But Apple has been working on making Face ID smaller and less obtrusive, as seen with the under-display IR camera on the iPhone 18 Pro. 

With iPhone Duo 2 and the twentieth anniversary iPhone Pro, we may see another evolution where both the IR camera and the flood illuminator go behind the screen, allowing the bezel or Dynamic Island cutout to be even smaller still.

	

Obviously, that just because they are testing the technology on iPhone Duo prototypes right now, it is not guaranteed that it will ship in next year’s revision. But it seems like that is what Apple is aiming for, so customers can probably expect it either next year or as part of the iPhone Duo 3, if development slips. 

On the same episode, Gurman also says that employees have been exploring ways to also bring the Action button to a next-generation model of iPhone Duo as well, although he seems less confident about this.

It’s also unclear if Apple would remove the Touch ID sensor from the power button if it adds Face ID to the device, or whether it would keep both methods of biometrics allowing users to authenticate whether they are looking at the inner or outer display.

title: Google reiterates missing Fitbit Air sleep breathing quality feature coming ‘soon’
snippet: Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month. more…
fullText:
Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month.

Under the Your Health Guardian umbrella of features, Google recently announced several new features for its fitness trackers. That includes not only the Pixel Watch series, but the Fitbit Air and even the newly announced Fitbit Edge. That suite provides access to blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality. 

The Fitbit Air has been left without one of these features since Google announced them – sleep breathing quality. Google recently stated, once again, that the Fitbit Air would get the features soon in a statement to Android Authority, this time more pointedly aimed at the missing function.

Sleep Breathing Quality launched first on Pixel Watches and will come to Fitbit Air soon.

When Google first announced these features, they made sure to include that detail in the press release so as not to get Fitbit Air users’ hopes up. At the time, Google said sleep breathing quality and other features in the Your Health Guardian suite would be added to the screenless tracker “later this year.” It didn’t note that only two of the three features would be released for the Fitbit Air.

	

That being said, neither the comment nor the original press release lays out a detailed timeline for sleep breathing quality trends, specifically. For now, the Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4, and Pixel Watch 5 are able to set sleep quality, insulin trends, and blood pressure trends on their devices with the Health Guardian feature.

Fitbit Air users will need to wait a little longer.

title: The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say
snippet: Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables. more…
fullText:
Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables.

Samsung provides display panels for both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, both of which have gained a massive amount of attention in the last couple of months. That’s credited to the form factor – a refreshing change from the tall and narrow Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or the devices that emulate the same experience.

Analysts at Omdia reported their forecast for 2026 in the wake of renewed interest in foldables, driven by Samsung and Apple. The report states that foldable AMOLED display shipments are expected to increase by 44% year-over-year. That includes shipments for any foldable displays, but it’s signaled by the surge of wide foldables released or rumored this year.

That increase would be driven by Samsung, if the prediction plays out perfectly. Samsung currently holds a majority lead in foldable display shipments, but it’s possible its slice grows to 66% in 2026. Omdia predicts that current Chinese manufacturers with high shipments will see a decline as demand from Apple and Samsung grows.

	

It’s unlikely we’ll see Samsung and Apple dominate the wide fold market. Motorola is expected to launch a similar foldable, and more will chase the size and shape Apple landed on for its first foldable iPhone.

One concern some users have had about iPhone Duo is that both the outer and inner displays are wider than on other iPhones. The UI also clearly favors right-handed use, as 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller confirmed in his review.

It sounds like for anyone who struggles to reach interface elements along the left or right edge of the device, iPhone Duo’s forthcoming Reachability feature should help.

title: Touchscreen Mac, or double your RAM or SSD size – what’s the better deal? [Poll]
snippet: We’re just a week away from the official announcement of the first ever touchscreen Mac. The upcoming MacBook Pro will also have an OLED screen, which may include a Dynamic Island, and is said to be lighter. We don’t yet know the price of the new model, but we can be sure it will carry a significant premium over the existing one. My guess would be somewhere in the $500 to $700 range … more…
fullText:
We’re just a week away from the official announcement of the first ever touchscreen Mac. The upcoming MacBook Pro will also have an OLED screen, which may include a Dynamic Island, and is said to be lighter. 

We don’t yet know the price of the new model, but we can be sure it will carry a significant premium over the existing one. My guess would be somewhere in the $500 to $700 range …

There’s so far been a fair degree of excitement about an OLED Mac. In some ways that’s certainly justified given the quality of the OLED screens we’ve seen on the iPad Pro. On the other hand, Apple’s IPS LCD panels with mini-LED backlighting have always looked fantastic, and I would say rival many competing OLED screens. For that reason, I’m expecting the improvement in display quality to be rather modest.

	

I’ve seen way less interest in the touchscreen. While there is certainly a segment of Apple fans who are eagerly awaiting it, the majority view seems to be that it will have limited utility and be a fingerprint magnet. My own experience of using a 12.9in iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard as a pseudo laptop is that I used the trackpad for everything except scrolling, so I don’t personally see much appeal in a touchscreen Mac.

A lighter MacBook is always welcome, of course, and if the weight difference is significant, that may be a reason to consider it. But unless it’s going to get somewhere close to the weight of a MacBook Air, it’s perhaps not worth such a substantial premium.

Assuming I’m right about the price premium, you’ll be paying somewhere in the region of $600 more for the new machine. For that much, you could double the RAM or double the size of your SSD when buying the existing model. Which would you consider the better deal?

Lighting effects can make or break your TV room, gaming setup, etc. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars take a different approach from most products, with dedicated cool-white and warm-white LEDs alongside the color zones. The end result means real white light for work and reading, and 12-zone RGBIC color for movies. It all works over Wi-Fi/Matter as well, so you don’t need a hub.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

RGB color mixing can produce something that technically looks white on a wall, but it’s not the same quality of light you’d want to read or work under for hours. If you work in an office building, you know what I am talking about. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars use separate cool-white and warm-white LEDs that produce actual white light with adjustable color temperature that can go from 2200K up to 6500K, and they dim as well. It can produce up to 800 lumens across the pair.

On the color side, each bar has six independently controllable RGBIC zones, so you have 12 zones across the pair. This lets you run multi-color gradients rather than a single color across the entire bar. There are 26 preset dynamic effects and six music-reactive modes powered by a built-in microphone, so you don’t need a separate sensor to sync the lights to sound.

Matter over Wi-Fi

The light bars connect to Apple Home natively over Matter via Wi-Fi without needing a SwitchBot Hub. The integration covers the basics: on/off, brightness, color temperature, and color control via the Home app or Siri.

The deeper color zone control, music modes, dynamic effects, and scene building all live in the SwitchBot app rather than Apple Home, which is standard for Matter accessories at this level of feature complexity. A wired physical controller is also included for quick changes to the lights as well. I am a big fan of when smart home products offer a physical button option as well.

The lights include built-in magnets so you can attach the bars directly to compatible metal surfaces, with adhesive being an option as well. They can be mounted horizontally, vertically, rear-mounted behind a monitor or TV, or set upright with the included desktop stands.

Wrap up

SwitchBot built just about everything you’d want here. The attention to color detail is fantastic. Matter over Wi-Fi means you can buy it and have it directly connected to Apple Home/HomeKit without a hub, while still having flexibility for the future.

title: The iPhone Duo Just Passed 20,000 in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
snippet: We’re folding Apple’s iPhone Duo 900 times an hour to test how its hinge will last.
fullText:
Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched Friday and was met with long lines and product sellouts. We braved three hours at the Apple Store on Friday to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

Now the big question? How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 1:30 p.m. ET on Saturday, we’ve just passed 20,000 folds.

The goal is simple. On Friday afternoon, my team and I loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone. 

		

			

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge. 

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience. 

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo. 

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube on Monday from 1-5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and ask questions about our iPhone Duo testing process.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day. 

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test. 

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Matthew Murray
						

						

							Lab Director						
					

										

								

											As lab director for the CNET Group, Matthew leads the Labs team, which helps coordinate and conduct product testing for CNET and other Ziff Davis editorial brands including PCMag and ZDNET. He previously spent eight years as head of testing at Future plc, and before that eight years as an analyst and writer at PCMag. His technology writing has also appeared in publications including Computer Shopper, ExtremeTech, Tom's Guide, Laptop and Backstage.

title: The real reason to care about Vivo’s latest phone is the camera [Gallery]
snippet: The Vivo V80 sports flagship design quality, a massive 7200mAh battery, Center-Stage selfie camera, IP68/69 ingress protection, and one of the wildest AI camera modes I’ve seen yet. more…
fullText:
The Vivo V80 sports flagship design quality, a massive 7200mAh battery, Center-Stage selfie camera, IP68/69 ingress protection, and one of the wildest AI camera modes I’ve seen yet.

When I think of the smartphone industry’s best cameras, Vivo or Oppo usually comes to mind. While both companies offer good experiences on any phone they sell, their best features often appear only on flagship models. But the Vivo V80, which retails for just ₹62,999 (~$660), features the company’s new flagship AI camera mode, and that might be the single most interesting thing about the release for me.

Let’s get the full specs out of the way first. The Vivo V80’s got a 6.59-inch 144Hz OLED display, featuring 1.5k resolution, true 10-bit colors (no dithering), and 4320Hz PWM dimming at low brightness (plus an option for full DC dimming). Inside is a Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, 8GB RAM, and that massive 7200mAh battery with 90W charging. Good stuff.

The Vivo V80 uses a main 50MP Sony LYTIA 700V sensor, a 3x optical 50MP Sony IMX882 telephoto camera, an 8MP or 12MP ultrawide camera (region-dependent), and a 50MP ZEISS center-stage 90-degree selfie camera. The phone is available in India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and other regions in the coming weeks.

	

To illustrate just how interesting the new AI Creation camera mode is, I took a bunch of photos using the same mode on the Vivo X500. That phone is about $300 more expensive, but it features the same AI Creation mode as the Vivo V80. The results are nothing short of jaw-dropping at times. Let’s start with the hike I took this weekend.

It was a gorgeous autumn day, but the sporadic cloud cover was really killing the vibe of my photos. The lighting was annoyingly flat, and the colors my eyes were seeing in the leaves weren’t being picked up on camera at all. So I swiped over to the AI Creation mode and hit the shutter button. The rest was all automated.

The amount of depth and color this mode added truly blew my mind. When you open the mode and point the viewfinder toward something, it scans the scene and automatically applies the style it thinks will be best. It’ll also give you two additional modes to quickly select from, or you can jump into the full UI and choose the one you want.

From here, you can also choose to have Vivo’s AI automatically remove anyone in the photo, and it does an impeccable job, too; no circling required! Original images are always available in Vivo’s Albums app, and you can select a different style after taking the photo.

This mode is 100% cloud processing, though, so you might need to wait to see the processing results if you were somewhere like I was with no signal. Processing takes about one minute per photo, and up to 10 images can be processed simultaneously. If there’s a processing limit per day, I didn’t find it. While the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 in the Vivo V80 could probably handle some of the processing, this ensures you get the best quality without much wait time.

The “Travel” category creates genuinely convincing effects like the Sunlight style. Vivo has several other options that are more dramatic and, therefore, obviously edited-looking. In the header image, I grabbed one of my son’s swords and asked him to take a picture of me. The sword and the room are fully real in these pictures, but the lighting and effects are all automatically generated by Vivo.

All of these, too, were quite convincing, despite obviously being stylized. I particularly love the mist one, although I’m not sure how often anyone would use most of these. They’re clearly only for niche dramatic photos, but hey, maybe you love that sort of thing. The rest of the options available under the “Landscape” category were initially convincing, but zooming in just a bit reveals some very obvious AI editing.

So all of this is amazing, but there’s one big problem that I’m not thrilled about: Vivo doesn’t use SynthID or another more standardized way of noting that these images are edited with AI. If you delve into the EXIF data, you can find “ai_creation” in the comments field, but Gemini apparently isn’t smart enough to understand that yet.

Most likely, Gemini and the rest will figure this out in time, but I don’t care much for AI editing tools that don’t automatically mark them as such. Vivo, if you’re reading this, please add SynthID or another way for AI tools to identify these as automated. Otherwise, this is a dope mode that I love seeing proliferate to more affordable phones like the Vivo V80, especially in the age of RAMageddon.

title: Some iPhone Duo displays are cracking, seemingly all in the same way
snippet: Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. more…
fullText:
Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). 

The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. 

The scale of the issue remains unclear. We’ve seen about ten unique instances so far, with many posting their (similar) experiences on the iPhone Duo subreddit. 

The amount of time it takes for the cracking to happen varies, but obviously it doesn’t take too long since customers have only been able to start unboxing the device since Friday morning. A couple of people even said theirs cracked during the first setup process. 

From what we’ve seen so far, most buyers experiencing this problem have been able to return to the Apple Store and get a straight device replacement. 

People who bought from carriers may have had less luck, as the carriers do not have immediate stock to give out a replacement. One person said they were told that they must have dropped the phone to cause the damage, and that it was on them to pay for repair.

	

In terms of why this is happening, there is a working theory that a batch of iPhone Duos have a defective hinge component. The suggestion is a piece of the hinge is slightly misaligned, and pokes upwards onto the inner screen, causing the breakage.

Some on social media have suggested that users should not close the iPhone Duo by pressing in the center of the inner display, and perhaps that contributes to this issue occurring. It is unclear if this is actually relevant advice. Officially, Apple has not given any guidance on how users are expected to handle the phone when folding and unfolding it.

While the reports are concerning, it is worth remembering that Apple has probably shipped hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of units already and only a small percentage of people have had their phone break on them. Hopefully, most people will be able to enjoy using their new iPhone Duo without issue. We’ve reached out to Apple for comment, and will update if we hear back.

title: Google explains how to fix time zones on Android amid changes in Canada
snippet: As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone. more…
fullText:
As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone.

When Daylight Saving Time comes to an end next month, parts of Canada will not be rolling back their clocks as the time change becomes permanent. Manitoba announced the change in September, with other parts of the country, including Alberta and British Columbia, also no longer changing their times twice a year, but different provinces and territories are making their own choices regarding which time to stick with.

Google, in a post, subtly acknowledges that things could get a little messy with these time zone changes and your Android phone.

Time is usually set automatically on Android, and it sounds like that will still happen for the most part. Google says to “apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device” if your phone’s time is incorrect on November 1 after the changes kick in.

	

But if there are still problems, you can make adjustments in the Settings of your Android device:

If you are still seeing an incorrect time or time zone, you can enable location-based time zone detection:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Enable “Automatic time zone”.

Enable “Use location for time zone”.

or set the time zone manually:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Disable “Automatic time zone”.

Choose “Time Zone”.

Choose “Region”.

Choose “Canada”.

Choose a time zone with the right offset.

title: TextNow’s $150 Yello Phone Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
snippet: The lower-cost phone has a parent portal for managing calls and texts, checking the phone’s location, and enabling games.
fullText:
Low-cost carrier TextNow launched its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized 2024 edition of the Moto G Play that costs $150 and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments. It’s a simple 4G-only Android phone with a 6.5-inch display, but TextNow makes a number of software changes to restrict most access to the internet.

The phone doesn’t include Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

			

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts.TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 50-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2024 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. Its 5,000-mAh battery should easily get through a day or two of use, and its IP52 certification should keep it resistant to light splashes of water. The phone has a limited amount of storage at 64GB, but that might work out fine considering the deliberate constraints placed on this device.

It’s worth noting that Motorola is only providing security support to this older model of the Moto G Play through 2027, but TextNow’s website says that its Yello software will continue to be built upon as the carrier gets user feedback. Since Motorola’s official support period for this phone is almost over, it will be important for TextNow’s Yello software to step in as it builds up features for this phone for kids.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same sapphire blue that’s on every 2024 Moto G Play.

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited that Yello was using a different edition of the Moto G Play. TextNow clarified the model after Yello’s announcement, and the story has been updated accordingly.
