title: These clever apps show off the iPhone Duo’s potential
snippet: From retro cassette players and virtual notebooks to flight trackers and even a digital toaster, developers are finding creative ways to take advantage of Apple's first foldable iPhone.
fullText:
It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone. 

For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable, or a new notch on the screen, but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was. 

The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect, is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. 

Image Credits:Apple

It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement, which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. 

Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad.

But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO. 

The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves. 

Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. 

Netflix 

Image Credits:Apple

Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical, and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV.

The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think.

Deck-Man (Formerly Duo-Man)

Image Credits:Deck-Man

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man, which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. 

Image Credits:Deck-Man

With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman.

The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech, which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech, like dumbphones, digital cameras, vinyl, CDs, and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.  

Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun. 

Duo-Man is now Deck-Man!

Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that.

See you October 23 on the App Store! pic.twitter.com/kCdjcmbeGG

— Vidit Bhargava (@viditb) October 14, 2026

TypeDraw

Image Credits:TypeDraw

The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed. 

Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut. 

Image Credits:TypeDraw

You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app.

The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.   

I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself.

Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH

— Phil Traut ᯅ (@SpatiallyMe) October 15, 2026

Wakeout

Wakeout, the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.

Image Credits:Wakeout

For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.) 

If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display.

Flighty

Image Credits:Flighty

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. 

The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. 

Image Credits:Flighty

Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. 

Tiny Computers

Image Credits:Tiny Computers

Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. 

You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. 

There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either –  just a $3.99 one-time fee.

Sky Guide

Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called.

The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. 

MD Vinyl

Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.

Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it.

Pico Cam

Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.

Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken.   

Honorable Mention, sorta: Toastie

Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience. 

I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid.  

The app, cheekily described as the “world’s most expensive toaster” (a reference to the Duo’s exorbitant price), lets you follow a recipe to create a piece of toast with butter, cheese, or any of the other numerous toppings, then close the Duo to let the toast cook. 

Open the phone too soon, and your toast will be undercooked, losing you the 5-star review you’re after. 

You definitely don’t need this app, but what’s another $2.99 when you’ve already dropped a bundle on the phone itself? 

We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead.

At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable, or a new notch on the screen, but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was.

title: Modretro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it?
snippet: As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways. more…
fullText:
As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways.

I have a decent number of original gaming consoles from the 90s, but the Game Boy is arguably the handheld that I covet the most. I was a little too young to really enjoy the DMG model, but the Game Boy Color was the first EDC I ever owned. It still has a special place in my heart that very few things can match.

Luckily for me, my parents didn’t throw my original clear “Atomic Purple” Game Boy Color away under the guise of ditching clutter at home. It’s a piece of art, one that I love dearly, but it’s missing out on the fundamentals of a good gadget by 2026 standards.

Using original hardware isn’t always ideal. You miss out on a backlit display, the battery longevity is often subpar, and, in the interests of hardware preservation, I don’t want to break something that means so much to me.

	

That’s kind of why I picked up the original Modretro Chromatic last year. That is a high-end FPGA Game Boy clone that replicates software emulation with hardware-level logic recreation. You’re able to play original cartridges with supremely accurate visuals, sounds, timing, all that good stuff.

The original Chromatic was kind of pricey at over $200 with the Sapphire glass display and all-metal chassis. Sure, those are “nice-to-haves,” but the new Modretro Chromatic Transparent lowers the price of entry and adds back in the transparent tech highlight of my youth for under $150 – with a copy of Tetris. Maybe you need to be a 90s kid to truly understand the appeal. I’m just glad that brands are at least offering us these kinds of options again.

I’ve been carrying this thing for a few weeks in my sidebag in place of my orange Chromatic, and it’s a different beast in many ways. Being able to play all of my favorite Game Boy games isn’t anything new, and sure, I could use an emulator on my phone, but there’s nothing quite like playing as Nintendo intended.

From a purely holistic standpoint, you’re going back to the slow, intentional gaming that is completely vanilla. Mod-free, methodical gaming that feels intentional. I love emulation as much as anyone, but playing at 1x speed rather than trying to speedrun the grinding of Pokémon is a throwback.

Okay, it’s not a gadget for everyone. It’s more of a fancy thing that old heads will adore because it literally does one thing exceptionally well. The screen is 1:1, and includes the all-important backlighting. It does downgrade the scratch protection to Gorilla Glass, but that is far better than what the original Game Boy could ever claim.

By default, it takes three AA batteries, or you can pick up a rechargeable battery pack that charges up through the USB-C port. The port does a little more, like letting you stream to Discord and update on-device firmware. Make no mistake, the Chromatic Transparent is made for the modern era, despite doing one thing and one thing only.

I was sent the green Chromatic Clear, and it’s almost jewel-like, which demands attention. I like that it isn’t quite neon; the smoky color feels premium despite the material difference from the original Chromatic. It will pick up scuffs and dings. Personally, I see that as a patina that means I’m playing my favorite games, which, in my opinion, we should all do more of. Although some of my original carts need battery replacements, I’m using a flash cart to play through my collection.

The buttons are not quite 1:1 with the original Game Boy Color. I’d say they’re a little “stiffer” but feel about as close as you could get without being outright replicas. I know some people won’t like the D-pad. It’s marginally harder to roll through the four directions than an actual Game Boy, so some games may play a little differently.

My only major criticism is that the volume scroll wheel is too easy to adjust without intent. So be aware that you might inadvertently increase the volume while launching the Modretro settings menu.

On that, the speaker is a solitary downward-firing mono speaker, and it gets loud with no distortion. It’s amazing to hear the earworm of the Tetris theme playing at full blast, but remember to tone the volume down when you’re in public.

For anyone wondering why you wouldn’t use an original Game Boy Color to play your games, well, that’s a very fair comment. However, to get a modded Game Boy Color that has all the same functionality, it actually costs upwards of $150 from most reputable sellers on sites like eBay. Modretro is basically undercutting the original with lots of quality-of-life changes with the Chromatic Transparent.

As much as I love this hardware and will covet it in my EDC, you simply cannot separate the company from the controversial founder, Palmer Luckey. To many, the ties to his business ventures outside the gaming space will tarnish the brand. I can understand hesitation, and while I was sent this device for review, you will need to decide for yourself if you are willing to support the company. It would be unfair to omit this; hence, mentioning it.

It would also be a lie if I were not to say I’m smitten with the product. I do wish it were not marked with this extra controversy, as it’s the best way for ardent retro gamers to play through your back catalog of Game Boy titles.

For $150, the Chromatic Transparent is not a cheap way to indulge in some nostalgia. However, it’s undercutting the competition and now has even better colors to choose from.

title: iPhone Duo orders limited to two per customer as Apple tackles scalping
snippet: Apple is limiting iPhone Duo orders to a maximum of two per customer in the US, UK, and elsewhere after shipping dates slipped into January of next year within minutes of pre-orders opening. The move appears to be an attempt to tackle the problem of scalping, where people buy large volumes of supply-constrained devices in order to resell them on eBay for well above the retail price … more…
fullText:
Apple is limiting iPhone Duo orders to a maximum of two per customer in the US, UK, and elsewhere after shipping dates slipped into January of next year within minutes of pre-orders opening.

The move appears to be an attempt to tackle the problem of scalping, where people buy large volumes of supply-constrained devices in order to resell them on eBay for well above the retail price …

Engadget reports that it tried to add more than two iPhone Duo units to its cart on the Apple stores in the US, UK, Japan, and Spain, and received a notification advising it of the limit.

We’ve tried adding more than two units to our cart on the Apple Stores for Japan, Spain and the United Kingdom, in addition to the US, and we’ve received a warning notice across all the online stores. The notification said: “A maximum of 2 iPhone Duo can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone Duo in your order before checking out.”

The site said that the same limit applies no matter what configuration you select.

The company is almost certainly implementing the move in a bid to reduce scalping. We’ve already seen dozens of iPhone Duos listed on eBay by scalpers, some with prices exceeding $5,000.

It’s not the first time Apple has imposed limits on supply-constrained iPhones. The company has done this in China multiple times, with limits applied to walk-in purchases in retail stores as well as those made online. The company has also done it in the US before, with the first example being the iPhone 5 way back in 2012.

9to5Mac’s Take

Industrial-level scalping is hard to defeat. Organized gangs use multiple virtual credit card numbers, email addresses, and delivery addresses in order to circumvent limits. Others pay people to place orders on their behalf.

All the same, it’s good to see Apple at least attempting to reduce the scale of the problem. It’s also possible the company is implementing other behind-the-scenes measures to detect and reject more sophisticated bulk purchase attempts.

As we predicted, some customers have seen improvements to their estimated delivery dates. It’s also worth trying for a walk-in purchase if you live close to an Apple store – just not on day one.

title: iPhone Duo one day later: Here’s why its quirks don’t make it any less incredible
snippet: Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks. more…
fullText:
Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks.

When discussing iPhone Duo, most people are going to talk about the under display FaceTime camera, Touch ID, and app support as compromises. Sure, those are features that make it a lesser experience than a typical iPhone, but personally, I don’t find them as experience-ruining at all.

Last year, Apple impressed many with the iPhone Air. It was incredibly thin, and certainly an engineering marvel to shove everything into that form factor. You felt it though: speaker quality was subpar, you only had a single rear camera, and battery life was lacking compared to any other iPhone. It was by no means unusable, but you had to compromise.

iPhone Duo feels like a full experience

To me, iPhone Duo doesn’t really feel like I’m giving up anything that really matters. Touch ID is a learning curve, but it doesn’t feel like a struggle. The under display FaceTime camera is worse than if it weren’t under display, but in good lighting it looks perfectly fine, especially over video calls.

As for app support, I feel the entire situation was overblown. Many early reviewers were quick to point out the fact that many apps aren’t yet updated for iPhone Duo, while ignoring the fact that they had the phone early and most developers were planning their releases for when consumers would start having devices, not reviewers. In just the past couple days, substantially more apps have been updated for iPhone Duo.

The outside screen also feels like something worth using, not just an afterthought. It’s a smaller screen, and you certainly read less on it than you’d otherwise be able to on a taller display. To me, though, the screen actually feels quite refreshing to use. The keyboard is still full width, you just don’t have to take in as much background context at once. It feels more focused.

That said, there are two things I’ve really felt with iPhone Duo that I’d like to see improved. Luckily, these are mostly software improvements.

Software suggestions

In the first day of using my iPhone Duo, I’ve noticed two things about the device that feel a bit odd. For one, iOS still only allows you to backswipe from the left edge of the device. This feels a bit in conflict with the fact that navigation elements are on the right side of the device. 

When I got my iPhone Duo, I found myself naturally trying to backswipe from the right edge many times. Unfortunately, Apple doesn’t let you do that. This certainly isn’t a make or break for the phone, and I’ve gotten used to reaching over to the left edge of the device, but given the fact that this form factor is otherwise incredibly reachable, I think that would be a nice adjustment.

Another thing I’d like to see improved is unlock with Apple Watch. The feature itself works great, and makes losing Face ID less of a pain. That said, it means if you hand your device to anyone else, they can just unlock it. I think having basic camera-based facial recognition in combination with unlock with Apple Watch would be a nice improvement.

Wrap up

Beyond that though, I’m incredibly happy with iPhone Duo, and I’m excited to use the device more over time and share my experience with you all. Anecdotally, I’ve never had so many people stop me in public and ask about my iPhone, so the Duo seemingly has people excited in a way I haven’t seen in ages. It’s a fun phone.

	

One last thing of note: Apple’s official folio case for iPhone Duo doesn’t seem like a worthwhile product. At $129, the kickstand doesn’t feel super strong, and the front flap creates an awkward situation when taking photos using the outside display. You can’t flip it around the back, since that’d cover the camera, so you just have to leave it floating. I’d skip buying this, and instead wait for third party solutions to fill the gap.

title: Apple is finally catching up with Siri, but the goalposts are moving again

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: Memoket Gem is a 0.4 oz AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch. One press captures a conversation, and KITE memory connects it to what you said weeks ago. 20-hour battery. Available now from $168.99 on memoket.ai and Amazon.

While it is great that Siri AI can finally deliver Apple’s promise of an actually useful, personal assistant for the age of AI, expectations surrounding agentic assistants are quickly shifting. But Apple is showing it might not watch from the sidelines again.

Siri AI is great, but it’s also very 2024

Now that Siri AI (which is still officially designated as a beta) has been out for a little more than a month, it seems fair to say that its two defining characteristics are that it’s finally useful, but it can be painfully slow to answer even simple queries.

And while I had spent the better part of the past few months mocking Silicon Valley’s obsession with AI assistants that can book flights and hotels, I hate to admit that the first time Siri AI actually impressed me was when I asked how much I’d paid for a hotel room for an upcoming trip to San Francisco and how far it was from my first appointment in the city. It got both answers exactly right.

Could I have looked this up myself? Sure. But setting aside the fact that I was in the middle of a 10K run at the time, finding that information on my own would undoubtedly have taken longer than it took Siri to give me the answers.

As a result, over the past few months, I’ve found myself increasingly relying on Siri AI for questions like “What was the contact information for that plumber who fixed the kitchen sink leak a couple of years ago?” or “What was the name of that PR person who introduced me to so-and-so?”

Information I know I have somewhere, be it an iMessage conversation or an email receipt, and that although I could just search for it, I’d now rather have Siri AI do it for me.

And for the first time in 15 years, I can ask these questions without already expecting Siri to fail halfway through asking them, only to get frustrated when it inevitably gets it wrong and proves me right.

That’s all well and good. The problem is that Apple has only now caught up with what AI assistants could do in 2024.

Apple’s next AI challenge: Building an agent harness for Siri

Particularly over the past few months, the frontier AI market has increasingly shifted toward agentic assistants, with products from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI (among many others) moving beyond answering questions to actually carrying out tasks on users’ behalf.

I subscribe to ChatGPT, and I’ve been using Codex and ChatGPT Work extensively for everyday tasks involving files and information scattered across my Mac and various cloud services.

And it still feels like magic every time I ask one of these tools to do something that involves opening, creating, editing, or organizing files on my computer, as well as interacting with websites and services I’m logged into, and it actually pulls it off.

The flipside of this is that every time ChatGPT completes one such task, the new Siri AI starts to feel like the old Siri all over again.

It is still early days, for sure, but it already feels like this is yet another area where Apple seems to be falling increasingly behind, as AI labs continue to improve their agentic capabilities, sometimes rolling out major updates just weeks apart, while Apple remains largely tied to its annual software release cycle.

But there’s one important limitation to today’s agentic assistants that I think Apple is particularly well positioned to address.

As impressive as tools like Codex, Dots, and ChatGPT Work can be, they still depend heavily on the user to provide the permissions and the context behind whatever task they’re supposed to accomplish. They can access files, search through emails, and interact with websites, but they generally don’t know what you’re doing, what you’ve been discussing with other people, or what you might need next unless you explicitly tell them.

And as these tools become increasingly capable of operating our computers and phones on our behalf, I suspect the next big leap in their usefulness will come not just from improving what they can do, but from improving their proactive understanding of the user’s context in real time.

That’s where Apple could have an advantage.

Apple has recently shown that it’s finally willing to capitalize on the trust it has spent years building around privacy, even if it means testing the boundaries of what users are comfortable sharing with an AI assistant.

Last month, it introduced two Apple Watch features: Siri Recap, which can automatically generate summaries of conversations throughout the day, and Live Rewind, which lets users retrieve the last 15 seconds of a conversation they may have missed.

Both features rely on the Apple Watch’s microphone to capture information about what’s happening around the user, potentially giving Siri access to an entirely new source of personal context.

Of course, the privacy implications are enormous, particularly because conversations involve other people who haven’t necessarily agreed to have their words processed by an AI assistant.

And while those concerns are certainly worth discussing at length (and are probably why these features have yet to roll out), Apple has repeatedly shown that it’s willing to go to extraordinary lengths to address the privacy challenges that come with giving technology access to sensitive personal information. Just look at the lengths it went to in developing its Reference Image system.

As agentic assistants become more capable, I suspect their biggest limitation will increasingly have less to do with what the underlying models can do, and more with how much we’re willing to let them know about us.

Imagine an assistant that doesn’t just wait for you to ask it to find a document or complete a task, but already understands what you’re working on. One that can gather information in the background so it’s ready when you need it, or even take action on your behalf based on what’s happening around you.

That’s the kind of assistant that could make today’s agentic tools feel as limited as the old Siri (and, increasingly, the new Siri AI) does now.

And while Apple still has plenty of catching up to do when it comes to actually building these capabilities, it is in a much better position to compete in this next phase of AI than it was when the generative AI race first began.

title: WhatsApp starts testing long-awaited scheduled messages on iPhone
snippet: After years of waiting, WhatsApp is finally making one of its most-requested messaging features available to select iPhone beta testers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After years of waiting, WhatsApp is finally making one of its most-requested messaging features available to select iPhone beta testers. Here are the details.

Scheduled messages are almost here

While Meta doesn’t generally break down active user figures by platform, Mark Zuckerberg said in April last year that WhatsApp had more than 3 billion monthly active users worldwide.

Ironically, despite being used by more than a third of the world’s population, WhatsApp still lacks some features competing platforms have offered for years. Case in point: the ability to schedule messages.

Earlier this year, WABetaInfo reported that code references in WhatsApp’s beta suggested the company was working on a message scheduling feature, although it wasn’t available for testing at the time.

Now, according to the site, the feature is finally rolling out to select iOS beta testers, less than two weeks after making its debut on Android beta.

Image: WABetaInfo

Here’s how the feature works, per WABetaInfo‘s report:

Users can schedule a message from the chat interface. After typing the message into the chat composer, they need to tap and hold the send button. WhatsApp opens the schedule message screen with a date and time picker. Users can scroll through the page and tap the green button at the bottom of the screen to confirm. The button shows the exact delivery time before users schedule the message. After scheduling a message, WhatsApp shows a confirmation in the chat, but it is only visible to the user who scheduled it.

WABetaInfo notes that messages can be scheduled as little as 10 minutes in advance or as far as two weeks in advance, and that scheduled messages appear in a dedicated section within the chat info screen or the group info screen for group chats.

Interestingly, in group chats, scheduled messages are only delivered to users who were already members when the message was scheduled. Anyone who joins the group afterward won’t receive it, even if they join before the message is sent.

The site also says that in addition to scheduling text messages, users can schedule messages containing photos, videos, and links. One current limitation, however, is that users cannot schedule multiple photos or videos at once, meaning each media item must be scheduled separately.

As is often the case with beta features, scheduled messages are only available to select testers, with no way to enable the feature manually. There’s also no word on when it will launch publicly, although with testing now underway on both iOS and Android, a wider rollout could be coming sooner rather than later.

title: A ‘Fallout’ Competition Series Is Coming to Prime Video
snippet: Get your Pip-Boy ready, Vault Dweller! Fallout Shelter: The Experiment is coming soon.
fullText:
Good news, Vault Dwellers. Prime Video on Friday announced that a new reality competition series, inspired by Fallout, Bethesda Game Studios’ hit video game franchise and Amazon’s sci-fi drama, will launch on its platform early in the new year.

Fallout Shelter: The Experiment is the official title, and its 10-episode season will drop the first four episodes on Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027, with three new episodes dropping weekly through Wednesday, Jan. 27.

“The world is ending,” the Pip-Boy animation in the short video announcement says. “The competition is just beginning.”

			

More from CNET

According to Amazon, Fallout Shelter: The Experiment will invite “everyday participants to test their aptitude for the apocalypse in Vault-Tec’s state-of-the-art bomb-proof vault shelters.” The series will pit the competitors against each other in “a series of high-octane drills, psychological dilemmas and morally challenging behavior trials” until there’s one person remaining to receive the grand prize of $1 million.

The timing of the announcement adds extra special meaning to Fallout fans, as Oct. 23, 2077, is known as Fallout Day in the fictional world of the video games and Prime Video’s series. This is the day that the bombs dropped, marking the beginning of the Great War that turned America into an irradiated wasteland. 

If you’ve ever wanted to live the Vault Dweller lifestyle, this show will probably be your cup of tea. Fallout Shelter: The Experiment is also the latest in a string of competition shows inspired by established genre properties; Netflix’s Squid Game: The Challenge and Wonka’s Golden Ticket come to mind.

Beyond the reality series project, Bethesda has announced fun global partnerships to commemorate the day, including a Fallout-inspired exhibit at the National Atomic Testing Museum in Las Vegas and the return of the Fallout Cafe to Tokyo’s Tower Records. The game studio also has a new collaboration with Jones Soda, titled Project T.W.I.S.T. (which stands for Taste-Worthiness Initiative for Shelter Transition), inviting people to help select the flavor for Nuka Twist — which will also reflect the Nuka Twist flavor, once it’s revealed in-game.

As for Fallout Shelter: The Experiment, the new spinoff project arrives at the beginning of 2027, which marks the 30th anniversary of the video game franchise (Fallout dropped on Oct. 10, 1997). With season 3 on the horizon, something tells me it’s going to be a big year for all things Fallout.

title: Apple keeps acquiring companies with one clear goal in mind
snippet: Apple acquires a variety of companies every year, and recently many of its acquisitions—including the latest, Samplab—have revolved around one clear goal: improving and expanding Apple Creator Studio. more…
fullText:
Apple acquires a variety of companies every year, and recently many of its acquisitions—including the latest, Samplab—have revolved around one clear goal: improving and expanding Apple Creator Studio.

Apple has prioritized Creator Studio with recent acquisitions, strengthening ecosystem for creatives

Next week, Apple is expected to unveil four new hardware products aimed at creatives: a redesigned MacBook Pro with touch, modernized iPad mini, and M6 versions of the iMac and MacBook Pro.

But hardware is only one part of Apple’s creator-focused push. 

All year long, the company has sought to strengthen its ecosystem of tools for creatives by launching Apple Creator Studio and acquiring companies that expand its feature set.

Apple Creator Studio debuted in January as a suite of pro apps for creatives, such as Pixelmator Pro, Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and more.

The service has regularly rolled out new features since launch, but we’ve also seen Apple invest behind-the-scenes with acquisitions that clearly have Creator Studio in mind.

In the spring we learned of two acquisitions that fit the bill. MotionVFX provided “visual effects templates, plugins, and motion graphics tools” for Final Cut Pro. Color.io brought tools for “color management and grading of digital imaging,” likely with Final Cut and/or Pixelmator in mind.

Now the latest acquisition revealed yesterday, Samplab, pitched itself as the “ultimate audio editor for musicians,” making its features a natural fit for Logic Pro. And even the recent acqui-hire of Huxe could have Creator Studio benefits too.

Why invest so much in Creator Studio? Obviously the chance to grow services revenue is reason enough. But I suspect the company also sees the app suite as a key component of its overall pitch to creatives.

Apple has long focused on bringing hardware, software, and services together in a seamless ecosystem. And its recent efforts on the software and services side are set to dovetail nicely with next week’s new hardware. All this to say, expect to see Creator Studio apps get some spotlight during Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ announcements on October 28.

Do you subscribe to Apple Creator Studio? If not, what’s it missing for you? Let us know in the comments.

title: iOS 27 adds new Phone app feature that’s an instant favorite

fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature puts key info on-screen when you’re on the phone with a business

I’m not a big fan of phone calls, so the Phone app isn’t somewhere I spend much time. But last year in iOS 26, the app had two of my favorite new features: Call Screening and Hold Assist.

Now with iOS 27 this year, Apple has again impressed me with a new Phone app feature.

Call Context is an Apple Intelligence feature that automatically surfaces relevant info on the call screen when you’re on the phone with a business.

Per Apple’s website:

Get relevant information while on a call. Call Context can proactively surface relevant information from across your apps when calling a business — like a confirmation code from Mail when you call an airline.

I’ve had the chance to use Call Context several times in iOS 27. And I’ve very quickly concluded that this is the kind of no-brainer addition that should prove popular.

Not long ago I booked flights with Southwest Airlines, and later needed to call them about a change.

When I called, my flight info was automatically put on the screen. My iPhone even offered to read the confirmation number out loud for me on the call.

iOS 27 was also smart enough to include details for another Southwest flight stacked underneath the foremost one. So if Call Context doesn’t show the most relevant info at first, in most cases it should be just a quick tap away.

Call Context is initially available only in English, and it’s limited to iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch models that support Apple Intelligence.

Have you tried Call Context in iOS 27 yet? How has it worked for you? Let us know in the comments.

title: LineageOS 24 review: Easier than ever to recommend [Video]
snippet: Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has. more…
fullText:
Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has.

LineageOS 23 review: The de facto AI-free alternative Android experience [Video]

It’s only been a few months since the LineageOS 23.2 drop, and we’re already here with the full-fat Android 17 release. The initial delays from Google last year might have lingered longer than we hoped, but the Lineage team has been hard at work, and version 24 is now ready to go.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Simpler installation process

The new online flash tool is, and I don’t say this lightly, the biggest upgrade to how you will flash the Lineage ROM on your devices in the history of the project. It is a fantastic addition and one that lowers the barrier of entry so drastically that it’s now a must for anyone with an older, unsupported handset.

	

However, even with a lower barrier to entry, you still need to follow the traditional flashing process, but it has been simplified. Just download the files and follow the correct order. Because the new method lets you do everything in a browser window, it makes it much easier to recommend – even more so if you already have Lineage installed on your phone.

Open a second browser window, follow the flashing process, and you will have LineageOS 24 running in a few minutes. Just remember that you will need to do a few things ahead of time. Back up your files, maybe restore your phone before you flash Lineage, and you can’t really go wrong.

I’m hopeful that in the future, it’ll be as robust and simple as the Android Flash Tool, but it’s one step at a time. This is still a huge improvement for accessibility.

We cover Google and all the platform updates here, but if you want to de-Google your life, you can ditch the GApps package. If you need the Play Store and Play Services, remember to download the MindTheGapps package before flashing. In the interest of trying LineageOS 24 as intended, we have omitted this from our own installation.

What’s new?

Like previous builds, if you choose to forgo the MindTheGapps package, there are no AI-powered functions unless you install those and link a Google account. If you want Circle to Search and Notification Summaries, then those will be missing unless you sideload those first.

More Material 3 Expressive and QPR1

LineageOS 24 has integrated a lot of the changes that were added with the QPR1 launch for Pixel phones back in September 2026.

App bubbles are the biggest headline addition. This may be limited to the default launcher on Lineage, but it mimics the pop-up floating chathead for your apps that you can stash on the left or right side of your phone display. The same 4 to 5 app limitation also applies, but the functionality is identical to what we’ve seen on Pixel phones.

Wallpaper and style gain the custom icon functionality, but don’t add anything extra. You can choose new shapes, the style, and disable app text labels. Sadly, we are still limited to just one lockscreen clock style, but you can adjust the text thickness to give it a different look.

The Expanded Dark theme has also jumped over so that apps that would ordinarily not have a dedicated dark mode will be themed, but darker tones are also used in apps that support the function. Your mileage may vary with this, so use with caution.

Animations and minor details all match the M3E changes added in QPR1, with all the latest icon changes and Quick Settings panel enhancements. There’s parity with the frontier builds of Android, but with the trademark LineageOS speed and fluidity on top.

Improved apps and controls

During the setup process, there is a system theme picker to get you set up before loading into the OS. I’m not entirely sure if this is new, but it felt like it had changed based on the Lineage 23.2 build I tested earlier this year.

The system update page looks much better, giving key information at a glance now. It’s a more robust section that helps you get updated and stay updated better than in previous versions of LineageOS.

Canvas, the default LineageOS 24 gallery app, is very simple, maybe a little barebones. It has gained some improved editing tools with this release. I do think they could be better, but they do include basic cropping and rotation. options. Basic markup is there with tools to scribble on your images if you need to do that. I haven’t used Snapchat for a while, but it reminds me of the old Snapchat editing toolset.

The Jelly default browser now supports PWA-lite or PWA-like apps when using the “Install shortcut” tool. I’ve found it doesn’t work all the time, but you can use it for services like Instagram and Spotify. It’s pretty useful if you want these lightweight web-based versions of an application, less tracking, and less space usage. This is a great addition.

The new Screen Recording UI is one such area that is improved with an option to record HEVC video directly from the floating panel. This is missing on Pixel phones and might be useful if you want to record high-quality but smaller video files locally.

One of the issues I still have with LineageOS is how the invisible gesture bar or hide feature has been enabled. Certain UI elements don’t fit when you have this disabled, so I would suggest keeping the hint enabled unless you don’t care about some elements feeling squeezed or shunted too close to the bottom display edge. It’s all personal preference at the end of the day.

LineageOS feels different now

I’ve been surface-level testing LineageOS for a good number of years now, and for the most part, I have always been impressed because the ROM gives you the ability to extend the lifespan of a phone or tablet that you’re still happy to use. I tend not to install on a brand new phone, as it defeats the purpose in my mind.

Outside market forces haven’t changed that one iota, but the ballooning costs of basically any and all technology have me thinking more about how flashing Lineage on some of my older devices is going to be a bigger component in my future.

My parents have older phones that are very close to the end of “official” support windows. I’m 100% going to be putting LineageOS 24 on those in the coming months. The peace of mind that comes with security updates and maybe even better performance is almost impossible to ignore now.

Extending the life of your possessions feels like the best way to say f-you to the big tech companies that have all banded together with the modus operandi that’ll we’ll all own nothing and be happy about it. At least there are options like this that still exist. I’m almost certain that I’ll be using this ROM more than I ever expected in the next few years across a wide array of devices I’m responsible for, and long may that continue.

To get started with LineageOS 24 and see all supported devices, click here.

fullText:

If you can’t get through the initial setup process on your smartphone, it might as well be an expensive paperweight. And that’s exactly the problem right now on some Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra devices, as a bug is causing the setup process to get stuck and leave the device unable to proceed.

Affected devices are left seeing an error saying that “the webpage is unavailable” for an account page on Samsung’s website. This seems to happen during setup, meaning you probably won’t run into the problem unless you reset your device.

Upon reviewing the details you provided, it appears there is an issue following the device UI 9.0 update. The development team has confirmed that this issue occurs when using an unstable system WebView on certain networks… 

Apparently, switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data can serve as a workaround, but your results may vary.

title: iPhone Duo’s software restricts an already-small display; Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn’t
snippet: Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware. more…
fullText:
Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware.

Samsung has struggled with the implementation of Android on its foldables. That’s the natural way of things as the form factor has progressed through the years. As the Galaxy Z Fold line has been refined, Google and Samsung have improved Android to be friendlier on big screens.

But this is Apple’s first try, and even on hardware that looks promising, iOS leaves something to be desired on the iPhone Duo.

This comes from a couple of second impressions. One short review via The Verge‘s Allison Johnson notes a couple of small complaints. The first details its usability. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo reportedly feels harder to use with one hand. Because the Fold 8’s taller and narrower physical presence, the cover screen is more easily navigable. That’s a big deal for those of us who gravitated towards the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for its unique outer screen.

	

The iPhone Duo also restricts that small 5.4-inch display by implementing a sidebar, which was intended to make navigation easier. But because the dock sits on the right side, there’s a big chunk of the display that’s essentially left unused. Another post on Twitter/X highlights the severe difference.

In The Verge‘s video, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is set to use a navigation bar instead of gestures, which makes the difference a little less blatant. But for those who use navigation gestures on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, there’s very little wasted screen space.

What Apple is trying to do with the iPhone Duo is to approach a small display with a space-saving solution. By shrinking the space allowed, you stretch media so it appears taller, like on a slab device. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 proves that leaving the space free for main content works pretty well.

The iPhone Duo is already available, but its availability is limited. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is continuing to prove a success for Samsung.

If you want to see more from Allison and 9to5Google, be sure to check out her appearance on our episode of The Sideload!

title: Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you
snippet: Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness. more…
fullText:
Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness.

Face Unlock as it exists on Pixel 8 and newer relies on the camera and Google’s software to deliver biometric authentication that’s actually strong enough to let you unlock secure apps such as banking and password manager apps.  

While the fingerprint sensor serves as a fine backup, not having Face Unlock in dark rooms can be a tiny bit frustrating. And Google’s solution appears to be just raising the screen brightness.

The folks over at Android Authority uncovered a new option being built out in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 which is simply titled “Brighten screen in low light.” Google’s summary of the feature reads:

	

Automatically boost screen brightness so Face Unlock works in dim lighting.

Sounds fun in a dark room.

An assortment of strings related to the feature further detail what to expect, with Google seemingly set to offer granular settings around if the feature is used when Bedtime mode, Do Not Disturb, or driving is detected, as well as a setting to tailor just how bright the screen can get.

“Reliable” sounds like it might turn up the brightness higher to ensure an accurate reading from Face Unlock, while “Comfortable” seems to trade brightness for, well, not blinding you. 

	

Some of the strings mention:

Brightness level – Reliable, Comfort – Lower settings may reduce reliability

Complete darkness – Can brighten to find your face when it’s too dark. When turned off, only brightens if your face is partially visible

Bedtime mode – Can brighten when Bedtime mode is on

Driving – Can brighten when a car ride is detected

“When this feature is turned on, the following accessibility settings may temporarily behave differently: extra dim, remove animations, or color inversion”

“Can brighten when Do Not Disturb is on”

It still doesn’t sound like a particularly elegant solution, but it’s certainly better to have the option available. As for when Google might roll this feature out, that also remains to be seen. 

Would you opt to have your screen brightness raise for the sake of using Face Unlock on a Pixel? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple blocks web certificates that could be used by scammers, but Mac vulnerability remains
snippet: Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites. However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … more…
fullText:
Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites.

However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … 

The issue concerns what are known as intermediate certificates. These are used to prove ownership of a website, so if you visit apple.com, for example, Safari will check that you are visiting the real site.

However, an error in a script used to generate these certificates led to a number of private keys that could be trivially discovered by testing just 256 possible numbers. The eight compromised certificates have now been revoked, and steps taken to ensure that the vulnerability won’t affect any future certificates issued.

Bleeping Computer reports that Apple, Google and Mozilla have each blocked the compromised certificates in their respective web browsers. However, Mozilla cryptography engineer Dennis Jackson warns that Macs may continue to trust them.

Jackson also warns that macOS’s built-in /usr/bin/curl utility may continue trusting the compromised certificates because its certificate bundle does not check revocation information.

In other words, if your Mac has already accepted one of the certificates, then it will continue to do so. However, there is currently no evidence of them being used in the wild, and it’s something that Apple is likely to be able to fix in an upcoming security update.

snippet: The popular retro game emulator Delta has today launched a big new 2.0 version, most notably featuring a refreshed Liquid Glass interface and support for the iPhone Duo. fullText:
The popular retro game emulator Delta has today launched a big new 2.0 version, most notably featuring a refreshed Liquid Glass interface and support for the iPhone Duo.

The app now has specially-designed controller skins that are optimized for all the different iPhone Duo poses, including some beautiful Nintendo DS layouts that use the full size of the inner display, and cleverly spans the crease when partially folded in book mode in portrait. 

The bigger screen of the iPhone Duo enables some immersive gaming experiences, but the Delta developers have also ensured that the app naturally reflows on the portrait closed outer screen too. 

Another little easter egg is that you can fold the Duo closed to automatically put the DS to sleep, emulating the physical behavior of a real DS console.

Delta also has a special trick when using it in landscape split view alongside another app. You can see it in action in this screenshot, which depicts Delta running side by side with another iPhone Duo app that is playing a video. 

Typically, the iPhone Duo Split View means each app is constrained to 50% of the screen space. But, as shown in this example, because the app exposes the bottom half of the virtual DS as a custom keyboard view, the system allows this ‘keyboard’ to stretch across the full width of the screen, overlapping the unrelated video player app on the other side of the split. 

Aside from iPhone Duo support, the new update also includes Sega Genesis ROM compatibility, improved library navigation, updated audio settings that allow game audio to mix alongside your currently playing music or podcast, and more. 

The premium version of Delta can be unlocked using an In-App Purchase subscription directly through the App Store, now available worldwide. In the US, EU, Brazil, and Japan, you can also support the app directly through Patreon.

title: YouTube removing ‘Subscriptions’ bottom bar tab on Android, iOS after nearly a decade
snippet: YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar. more…
fullText:
YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar.

On mobile, YouTube is “kicking off a series of updates to shape a more seamless Home experience.” This starts with a redesigned top bar with dedicated feeds.

As part of this change, YouTube is removing the Subscriptions tab from its fourth position in the bottom bar. It’s now in the “top bar on the Home tab.” Testing of the redesign started earlier this year. 

“Subs” appears in the second position after “Home” with a red underline that will take some getting used to. This change will break a lot of muscle memory, with Subscriptions appearing in the YouTube bottom bar for nearly a decade (2017).

	

Old vs. new

Meanwhile, after Subs, you’ll see new dedicated feeds for Live, Music, and Movies & TV, with the latter only appearing if you have active subscriptions (such as Primetime Channels). This change has the upside of removing YouTube’s navigation drawer. 

	

More broadly, this change coincides with the launch of custom feeds, which are also available on and sync to the web. This lets you describe “what you want to see in your own words”.

Tap “+” at the top of your Home feed and describe the topic, channels, or vibe you’re looking for (for example, “help me unwind after work with guided meditations under 10 minutes”). You’ll then get a new feed tailored to your interests for you to explore.

They will appear as top tabs in the main feed after Home and Subs so that “you can jump back into them whenever you want.” The prompt box at the top of each feed lets you change it.

Notably, free users “can save up to 3 active custom feeds, while YouTube Premium members can save up to 8.”

Custom feeds are first rolling out on “mobile and desktop in English to U.S. based, signed-in viewers.” It will be available in more countries going forward.

title: Some Galaxy S24, S25 owners say Samsung’s latest update is wrecking battery life
snippet: Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.” more…
fullText:
Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.”

It’s an age-old story. Major update on a last-gen device and battery life, at least for some users, gets worse. It’s something you hate to see, but it’s a pretty established pattern at this point. 

Reports have popped up since the update started rolling out more widely. SammyFans spotted a report of one user whose phone died in just over 5 hours, admittedly on heavy use. Other reports we found on Reddit include increased idle battery drain. Meanwhile, there are also reports on Galaxy S25 series devices, including one user who now has to “charge my phone 3 to 4 times a day,” with others mirroring that problem. 

This seems to be the oddity and not the norm, so far at least. These reports aren’t widespread, nor are droves of other users reporting the exact same problem. Some troubleshooting steps that can help range from a simple reboot, force-stopping rogue apps, or a factory reset. Major system updates like this, as mentioned, just tend to go a little rogue sometimes. 

	

Let us know in the comments if you’re running into any issues!

title: Someone built iPhone Duo’s tent mode for Android foldables, but made it even better
snippet: Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing. more…
fullText:
Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing.

One iPhone Duo feature that isn’t widely used on Android is the ability to show information while in “Tent Mode.” The Motorola Razr Fold is one of the few book-style foldables with this feature as a part of its always-on display, but the iPhone Duo’s “StandBy” mode is one that folks could easily want on other devices. Pixel also has similar functionality, but only while charging. 

A new Android app that delivers something pretty close to iPhone Duo’s tent mode is “Foldy.” 

The app is free to use, but requires a premium unlock (90¢/month or $9 lifetime) for its most useful features. On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app quickly let me turn tent mode into a useful dual-pane hub that shows the date and time, or data from my calendar. 

	

Its most useful functionality, though, is the ability to turn any Android widget into a pane, opening the door to useful functions such as Google Home or music app controls.

“Foldy” also lets you “train” the app to know when to activate. This works very well, with the app recognizing when the device is partially open and on its side, activating the “StandBy” clone as soon as the conditions are right.

Another example of Android developers quickly coming up with their own takes on iPhone Duo apps is “Foldman,” an app that turns your foldable into a Walkman-style casette player. It’s similar to a Duo app that’s been widely talked about, but with some added bonuses such as YouTube Music integration.

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music

Is this a bad thing? No! One of the biggest benefits that Apple’s entrance to the foldable space was going to bring was helping to build out new app experiences for Android foldables. I can’t wait for this sort of effort to expand to many more Android apps and experiences.

title: YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening
snippet: Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is. more…
fullText:
Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is.

The dislike button has been a topic of contention in the YouTube community for years now, ever since YouTube removed the count that showed alongside it. So when some users noticed that the dislike button was suddenly no longer visible and hidden behind an overflow menu, there was plenty of confusion around the change.

In a statement to 9to5Google, though, YouTube directly confirms that this is not a test or a change that you’ll see on YouTube videos. Rather, this update to the dislike button’s location appears solely on the video page for a creator’s own video. In other words, you’ll only see this altered location on your own videos.

A YouTube spokesperson explains:

	

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

And, sure enough, we were able to immediately replicate this behavior when we tested it out on one of our own videos.

title: I needed a dashcam while out running. Meta glasses turned out to be the answer
snippet: I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair. more…
fullText:
I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair.

This summer, I did something I never thought I would do: I started running. “But Nick, why are you running if nothing is chasing you?” my friends joked snarkily. The reality is, yes, I do often run a little faster at times to avoid getting hit by a car, something that’s particularly problematic any time I have to cross a road (even if there’s a crosswalk).

That got me thinking. If cars have dashcams, what could someone do to help document a potential accident? There’s no chance I’m running while holding my phone, and I wouldn’t want it in my pocket either. I also wouldn’t be able to pull it out of one of those armband holsters fast enough to video a potential accident, either. Then I realized the answer was already on my face: my Meta glasses.

I’d already been taking my glasses out on every run to make short video clips to post to my Strava account — with my smartwatch health stats plastered on the video, too — so it made a lot of sense to just take a few more clips along the way. Now I have a personal running dashcam at all times, and it takes less than a second to capture a video whenever I need it.

	

Is this really convenient?

Maybe surprisingly, yes, using Meta glasses as a dashcam is quite convenient. Since I already wore my Meta Nova and Oakley Meta HSTN glasses on regular runs, I didn’t have to significantly change my behavior. I already look out for cars when I cross the street (my mama taught me well); all I have to do now is hold the camera button to start a video recording if I see one coming.

I’ve got my Meta glasses set to record 3 minutes at a time, so I’m not worried about missing a potential problem because the recording got cut short. Once I cross the road, I just press the button again and manually stop the recording.

	

Everything is saved to the glasses until it reconnects to my phone; then everything is synced automatically at that time. It’s as effortless as you can get, and it’s impressively good insurance if anything were to go awry on a run.

If I had to buy a new pair of Meta glasses today, there’s little chance I’d buy one without a camera. While there’s been some negativity surrounding the inclusion of the camera, there are far too many good reasons to have it available to use.

Runners who want to try this should give the Oakley Meta HSTN glasses a shot first, as they’ve got the tightest fit and the most “runner-like” style. Otherwise, the cheaper Meta-branded glasses (read: no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding onboard) are a better budget choice, especially since there’s no functional difference between any of Meta’s latest pairs. And, if you really want to stay away from Meta, Rokid AI Glasses are the best alternative I’ve used to date.

title: tvOS 27.2 adds three new features to your Apple TV 4K
snippet: tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Shuffle option for screen savers

tvOS offers a variety of great screen savers across multiple categories, including Aerials, Memories & Slideshows, Portraits, and Snoopy.

But historically, you’ve had to choose just one of these categories for your Apple TV screen savers, thus missing out on all the others.

In tvOS 27.2, Apple has a new ‘Shuffle’ option which will cycle through all available screen savers—regardless of category—throughout the day.

I’ve always favored Apple’s beautiful selection of Aerials. But I love that now I can continue enjoying Aerials while also benefiting from the other screen saver categories too.

#2: Apple TV app supports sign language

title: Apple must open iPhone to alternative app stores in Australia after Epic Games ruling
snippet: An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
An Australian federal judge has ordered Apple to make sweeping changes to its App Store rules following a years-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. Apple has confirmed that it plans to appeal. Here are the details.

Epic scores major victory in Australia

Apple must allow iPhone users with Australian Apple Accounts to install apps from third-party app stores and websites starting March 1, 2027, a federal judge ordered today in a 235-page decision. Apple has until February 15 to request an extension until May 3, 2027, subject to court approval.

Today’s order follows a ruling last year that Apple violated Australian competition law by restricting alternative app distribution and payment methods, in a lawsuit brought by Epic Games similar to its long-running legal battle with Apple in the US.

In his decision, Justice Jonathan Beach said Apple held “a substantial degree of power in the iOS app distribution services market and the iOS in-app payment solutions market,” and used its developer agreements and App Store guidelines to restrict competition.

Among the practices singled out by the judge were:

Blocking app downloads and installations outside the App Store

Preventing developers from distributing apps through alternative channels

Requiring developers to use Apple’s in-app payment system

Prohibiting links to alternative payment methods

Requiring developers to offer content purchased elsewhere through Apple’s in-app purchase system as well.

Preventing developers from handling refunds directly

The ruling also cited Apple’s actions against Epic Games in 2020, including its refusal to allow Epic Direct Pay, Fortnite’s removal from the App Store, and the subsequent termination of Epic’s developer account.

Justice Beach described the latter two actions as “a paradigm example of Apple’s enforcement of its restrictive terms, in contravention of” section 46 of Australia’s Competition and Consumer Act 2010, which prohibits corporations with substantial market power from engaging in conduct that has “the purpose, or has or is likely to have the effect, of substantially lessening competition” in that market.

As a result, Justice Beach issued a wide-ranging series of orders requiring Apple to, among other things:

Allow alternative app stores and sideloading: Let Australian iPhone users download and install apps directly from websites and third-party marketplaces.

Allow alternative payment methods: Let developers use payment systems other than Apple’s, including within apps distributed through the App Store.

Permit external payment links: Allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods from within their apps.

Provide access to developer tools: Make the APIs and tools necessary for alternative app distribution available on substantially the same terms as those offered to App Store developers.

Restrict fees and other barriers: Prohibit fees for accessing alternative distribution channels, limit certain fees on external payments, and allow developers to offer lower prices outside Apple’s payment system.

Readmit Epic Games’ apps: Allow Fortnite and other eligible Epic Games apps back onto the Australian App Store, subject to compliance with applicable developer rules. (Importantly, this specific order is not subject to the March 2027 deadline, but rather takes effect immediately, with Apple required to act upon receiving a written application from Epic.)

The decision also addresses several other aspects of Apple’s App Store policies, including restrictions on its ability to turn off apps installed outside the App Store and requirements related to notarization.

The court also prohibited Apple from requiring developers to report transactions processed through alternative payment providers or offer Apple’s payment system alongside their preferred alternatives, both of which are requirements the company imposes in other regions, including Brazil and Japan.

When it comes to Apple’s wins in the decision, the list is much slimmer. Judge Beach rejected Epic’s request to extend the court’s injunctions worldwide and allowed Apple to maintain security scanning and notarization requirements for apps distributed outside the App Store. And while Apple must permit competing app marketplaces on iOS, it is not required to distribute them through its own App Store. This is a distinction he had already established in last year’s ruling.

Finally, the court ordered Apple to pay 85% of Epic’s legal costs incurred through the original trial, while reserving a decision on costs associated with the subsequent hearings over remedies.

	

Commenting on the decision, Epic confirmed “Fortnite is coming back to the App Store in Australia tomorrow,” and celebrated it as “great news for developers worldwide and iOS users in Australia who will benefit from an open mobile app ecosystem.”

In a statement to Reuters, Apple said:

“We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution ​that ​respects our ⁠intellectual property and protects the safe, ​secure experience that consumers ​and ⁠developers expect from the App Store.”

title: Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music
snippet: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon.

Foldables sort of walk that dichotomic line between nostalgic and futuristic. They remind us of flip phones from the 2000s, while running on an entirely different decade of tech.

Naturally, a Walkman-style app is a welcome addition to something like the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

One user developed an app called “Foldman” that uses your music from local storage or other apps and plays them in a virtual tape deck. On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app’s facade looks just like a cassette player. The app expands to show a wider stereo visual when the phone is opened up.

	

There’s a ton of cool little touches, like a volume slider and running tape counter on the virtual player. And the tape actually transfers from one tape reel to the other instead of a looping animation with no progressive movement! That’s such a nice little detail.

A Walkman-esque app fits so well on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 because of how wide and short the front display is, just like Sony’s original cassette player. That form factor is becoming increasingly popular, and it’s creating opportunities for some cool apps like this.

The app’s developer plans to integrate Spotify within the next couple of days and cautions that this early version has some rough edges. For now, it works with YouTube Music and Apple Music, as well as with files stored locally. The app is free and open source, stripped of ads or tracking.

We never recommend users download APKs outside of verified app stores, so do so at your own risk.

Beyond Spotify, they note that they’re looking into adding support for self-hosted streaming services, so users can use it with their existing library of digital files on their network. For now, it’s a simple little Walkman-style player, and that’s cool enough.
