title: I Caved to the TikTok Trend of Cooking Bacon in Water. Here’s How It Went
snippet: Water and greasy bacon sound like a recipe for hot splatter. Here’s how the viral hack actually works.
fullText:
Bacon has become a mainstay on American breakfast plates. This cured, often-smoked pork product, cut mostly from a pig’s belly, adds a one-of-a-kind crunch and savoriness to breakfast, providing a salty counterpoint to other signature dishes like scrambled eggs, pancakes and oatmeal. 

We all have bacon preferences: charred and crisp, soft and chewy and, for most of us, somewhere in the middle. Regardless of the outcome, a trending TikTok cooking hack claims to at least guarantee even cooking, prevent dangerous, dirty oil splatters, and keep the meat from burning beyond recognition. But does it hold up? I put the viral video tip to the test. 

The water-cooked bacon process

Though I’m a fan of the quick, easy, CNET-approved oven-baking technique and even speedier air fryer method, the water-cooked method allegedly renders the bacon’s fat slowly and consistently, resulting in uniform cooking, fewer splatters and even reduced sodium. 

			

More from CNET

Here’s how it works.

The technique couldn’t be simpler.Joey Skladany/CNET

The stovetop process is simple: 

Place bacon slices in an oversized skillet so they lie flat. 

Add ¼ cup of water to the skillet and cook over medium heat. 

Allow the water to steam and evaporate. Once the water is gone, lower the heat to medium-low and cook the bacon until it reaches your desired crispiness. 

Remove the cooked bacon from the skillet and place on a paper towel to soak up excess oil. 

I assumed the water would cause grease bombs, but it did the opposite. Joey Skladany/CNET

Ultimately, the water is said to suppress hot grease from popping violently and landing on stovetops or, more importantly, your skin. It also lets the meat cook low and slow before it fries in its own grease, rather than crisping immediately as the skillet heats up.  

Water can also draw out some of the bacon’s sodium, which is ideal for those who find it too salty. 

The results

The bacon turned out crisp with a slight chew.Joey Skladany/CNET

Color me shocked by the results: This cooking tip was executed flawlessly and lived up to the hype. The bacon strips were chewy yet crispy, with no bitter char, and cleanup took mere seconds with a quick wipe with a sponge and towel. (Pro tip: Reserve the leftover bacon grease to cook everything, from vegetables to rice, for added flavor). 

My only gripe was that it took a few minutes longer than using an oven or cast-iron skillet. And, frankly, the clean-up of pesky splatters would far surpass the time it takes to cook with water, at least with the latter tool. 

TikTok cooking tips are a mixed bag, but this bacon hack proved itself a winner.Joey Skladany/CNET

In an industry full of gimmicks and unverifiable shortcuts, it’s nice to sift through the culinary fluff and find something that actually works, especially with an ingredient as universally beloved as bacon. The fact that this trick has trended on TikTok is just a footnote and proof that social media sometimes gets it right. 

Hungry for more tips? Here’s how to recycle frying oil, plus a neat trick for degreasing a frying pan before washing.

title: iPhone Duo Owners: Your Apps Will Look Better Soon
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has new screen dimensions, leaving apps with a lot of unused space or awkward cropping. It’ll get better over time.
fullText:
For some lucky Apple superfans, today is the day they get to unbox their iPhone Duo. (Others may have to wait until January.) But after formally transferring all their software, they’ll discover a troubling truth: Some of their favorite apps look bad, with awkwardly unused space. 

Yet the message from CNET phone reviewers over the decades is reassuring. If precedent is anything to go by, updates will be coming to adjust apps to the iPhone Duo’s novel screen ratios, from the squat and wide front screen to the 4:3 inner display. Don’t worry — your apps will get better (and some are already tuned to the device’s dimensions).

That may be little comfort for Duo owners looking forlornly at Android foldables, which have had the better part of a decade on the market for app makers to adjust to the new formats. Despite having a similar passport-sized format to Apple’s foldable, most apps are sized correctly for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

But that wasn’t the case with the first Samsung Galaxy Fold, which launched in early 2019, as CNET Editor at Large Andy Lanxon recalls. 

“I had exactly the same experience when I used the first Samsung Galaxy Fold on the day it came out, with many apps appearing to be oddly squashed into that larger inner display,” Lanxon said. “Over time, both Android and foldable makers like Samsung and Google developed better software to accommodate foldables, and I’m confident that Apple won’t take long to patch up any shortcomings in this area.”

		

			

Indeed, it’s easy to forget that as the world’s first mainstream foldable, the original Galaxy Fold launched with plenty of display, hinge and other hardware problems that were ironed out over the years. Apple’s first foldable benefits from that refinement, launching with a minimal crease, a smooth and seemingly durable hinge, internal software suited to a folding screen (with FOMO-inspiring animations), IP68 dust- and water-resistance and other qualities that ease use.

The Duo also benefits from being a single design, as opposed to the various screen sizes and formats across all the Android foldables. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, for instance, both have 6.5-inch outer screens and 8-inch inner screens, but the former is slightly wider yet shorter than the latter. 

Read more: New iPhone Duo? Here are 4 Features You Should Check Out Now

The iPhone Duo’s inner and outer screens have the same ratio.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

But it’s the Duo’s specific design that might also accelerate app adjustment, Lanxon notes: The outer display has the same aspect ratio as the larger inner display, something Apple highlighted during its Sept. 9 presentation launching the device. So developers only need to design one app size for the Duo that will work perfectly well on both displays. 

Compare that to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which pairs a tall and narrow 21:9 cover screen with an almost square 10:9 inner screen.

That’s somewhat reassuring, but what iPhone Duo owners likely want to know is: When will my apps get updated? To predict that, we look to the past — both the development of other foldables and the radical changes in Apple’s own iPhone line.

The iPhone X, revealed on stage in October 2017, shifted to an all-glass front panel and the notorious notch at the top, requiring apps to adjust. 

Apple / Screenshot by Sarah Tew

Remembering when apps had to adapt to new screens

Given how long smartphones have had all-glass front panels, it’s understandable that it takes time to adapt apps to foldable displays. But it’s easy to forget that app makers had to go through the same process before when phones finally ditched physical buttons below screens for the all-glass front to begin with. 

“I remember when the iPhone X came out, and apps that hadn’t been optimized had black bars above and below,” said CNET Editor at Large Scott Stein, who reviewed the device back in 2017. “It meant all apps didn’t initially make the most of the new phone’s size.” 

The Duo will have the same growing pains until more apps get optimized, Stein added — it takes time, and it’s part of what it means to be a hardware early adopter. 

The original Samsung Galaxy Fold, launched in Feb. 2019.

Sarah Tew/CNET

It’s important to remember how complex it is to make software for a foldable, as explained by Jessica Dolcourt, CNET Group and CNET Labs vice president of content operations and commerce. When you open and close a foldable device, you’re asking your app to perform acrobatics, instantly leaping between internal and external displays while simultaneously expanding or contracting the view window and rearranging all the pixels. 

Dolcourt spent over a decade reviewing phones for CNET, including the original Samsung Galaxy Fold in 2019, where she got her first taste of apps rendering badly.

“Native apps could be slow to load, but brought the vision of a foldable future to life. Third-party apps — which were most of them — struggled to catch up quickly and smoothly to the demands of a folding screen,” Dolcourt said. “At the outset, some were barely usable.”

Nowadays, most apps are designed for Android foldables, in part thanks to years of Google software updates specifically addressing flexible displays. The Duo will have to play catch-up. 

But as Lanxon pointed out, Apple has deep relationships with developers of its apps, which sometimes launch on iOS first before heading to the Google Play Store. Apple will surely be working closely with its software partners to ensure they’re using the Duo’s proportions to the best advantage, Lanxon said. 

When your apps, like Instagram, will be updated to fit the Duo’s screens is hard to gauge (especially given it took 15 years to get an iPad-native Instagram app), but developers have many more advantages than they did when adapting to the first Android foldables’ displays. Over time — and hopefully soon — the Duo will be even better to use as apps catch up with it.  

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. As a true Californian, he lives for coffee, beaches and burritos.

title: iOS Decoded: iOS 27.2 RC – hands-on w/ HomePod Sound Glow, TV profiles, Apple TV Home Theater assets, more [Video]
snippet: In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap. We also go hands-on with other changes, like the handy new profiles option for the TV app and Suggested Actions for Messages. Further, we take a look at and listen to some of the assets and sounds from Apple TV’s new surround-sound Home Theater functionality. Watch our full hands-on video as we dive into these changes and many more, and be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more. more…
fullText:
In this episode of iOS Decoded, we take the HomePod’s new Sound Glow feature for a test drive and try out the new Lock Controls feature to prevent accidental activation of its top cap.

We also go hands-on with other changes, like the handy new profiles option for the TV app and Suggested Actions for Messages. Further, we take a look at and listen to some of the assets and sounds from Apple TV’s new surround-sound Home Theater functionality.

Watch our full hands-on video as we dive into these changes and many more, and be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more.

Sound Glow

Starting with iOS 27.2, the HomePod mini and 2nd-generation HomePod will see their LED Matrix displays, which feature 19 and 37 RGB LEDs, respectively, used in a way they haven’t before, thanks to Sound Glow.

Sound Glow transforms the top cap into a color-matched animated visual canvas that matches the album artwork. The canvas glows and pulses in concert with the currently playing song or podcast, responding to changes in bass and treble. For Soundscape ambient sounds like rain, forest, fireplace, etc., bespoke RGB animations are used instead of the Sound Glow audio processing pipeline, since Soundscapes are very different from music.

Video: iOS 27.2 Top Features

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Users who have updated their iOS devices and HomePods to 27.2 will find a new Sound Glow toggle in the Home app under the HomePod settings.

I’ve tested Sound Glow fairly extensively, and I’ve been impressed by the feature. It gives music playback a slightly unique experience with each song. I’ve also been impressed by the sheer vibrancy of the display, as Apple is clearly making full use of all of the LEDs embedded under the top cap to generate unique colors based on the currently playing song.

Sound Glow is vibrant, but it’s not extremely bright, and won’t light up your room or anything. But if you place your HomePod in an area where the top cap is easily visible, it’s a really nice addition.

What’s more noteworthy is that Sound Glow isn’t just limited to new hardware like Apple’s recently announced HomePod mini 2. The feature also works with the first-generation HomePod mini and the second-generation full-sized HomePod. 

We’ve long known about the LED Matrix display that sits under the touch sensor, but it makes you wonder how long Apple has been sitting on such a feature internally, before deciding to announce it during the HomePod mini section of Apple’s recent HomeView hardware unveiling. My takeaway: Sound Glow may look simple on the surface, but there’s a lot of impressive engineering under the hood that generates these animations!

Lock Controls

Another new HomePod-focused feature found in iOS 27.2 is the ability to lock the touch surface to prevent both accidental and intentional interactions. Users will find a new Lock Controls toggle when opening the HomePod settings inside the Home app. Enabling this feature will disable touch interactions for touch, touch and hold, and volume controls.

When touching the top cap with Lock Controls enabled, you’ll see a red animation that shakes back and forth, as if it’s saying “no”. 

The red “no” indicator when using the touch panel with Lock Controls enabled

As I mentioned in the video walkthrough above, my cat sometimes paws at the top cap, causing the HomePod to play music. Enabling Lock Controls would eliminate that issue while still allowing human household members to control Siri by voice or via another iOS device.

In addition, Apple notes that Lock Controls will not interfere with the ability to interact with features such as timers, intercom alarms, check-in, or FaceTime calls via touch. All of those items will remain responsive to a touch of the top cap.

Apple TV Profiles

The TV app on iOS 27.2 now supports creating new profiles and switching between them, something we’ve already been using on tvOS. This feature is especially useful if you have small children who enjoy using your phone to watch content via the TV app. Now you can simply switch to your child’s profile, and they can enjoy their content without affecting your profile. In other words, no more episodes of Duck & Goose or Frog and Toad littering your Up Next queue.

TV app profiles come in handy when sharing your device with kids

Suggested Actions

The Suggested Actions feature for the Messages app first appeared in the initial iOS 27 betas but was eventually removed before iOS 27 shipped. Now, in iOS 27.2, Apple is ready to ship the feature that will automatically suggest actions based on what’s in your Messages thread. For example, if you paste an address, you might receive an Open in Maps suggestion, or if you type in a date, an Add to Calendar suggestion may appear.

Messages suggestions return for the first time since the iOS 27 beta

Users can fine-tune the types of suggestions presented in Settings → Messages → Suggested Actions. There, you can toggle on or off add to Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Show in Maps, and Flight and Packages suggestions. Apple also notes that suggestions that you don’t use will stop appearing after a month.

Apple TV Home Theater setup

We’ve discovered lots of interesting new assets that give us a behind-the-scenes look at the setup process for the fourth-generation Apple TV’s Home Theater capability, made possible by adding four HomePods in two separate stereo pairs.

A look at the different HomePod Home Theater configs with Apple TV 4th-generation

We also get a look at some of the animations used during that process, along with an impressive-sounding Celebration animation upon successfully calibrating your Home Theater. You can listen to the corresponding sound just below:

9to5Mac’s Take

These features are just the tip of the iceberg in terms of all that we uncovered in the iOS 27.2 beta. In our hands-on video, we discuss details about unreleased iPhone and iPad hardware we found. I let you hear and see lots of new sounds and assets from the HomeView setup process, and more. Stay tuned for future episodes of iOS Decoded, where we go deeper than the surface level in terms of new iOS releases!

title: iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth.

Ahead of the first shipments arriving for customers later this week, the avalanche of iPhone Duo reviews has arrived today and, with it, the first look at what it’s like to live with Apple’s first foldable. 

Starting with our sister site 9to5Mac, of course, Chance used the iPhone Duo for a week and walked away “convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone.” His in-depth review hits on every key aspect of this device, but his ultimate conclusion boils down to this being the future of Apple’s smartphones because the form fact “just makes sense” and that there’s “something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience.”

9to5Mac: iPhone Duo review: The future is foldable

Looking at iPhone Duo reviews from the perspective of someone who’s been using Android foldables as their daily driver for over half a decade at this point, I can’t help but look at Apple’s first attempt and see the foundation it’s building on, but also the places where Apple’s inherent polish comes into play.

	

One big part of that seems to be the inner display. The nanotexture matte finish sounds like a big deal, with it making the crease visually not a problem. It’s still there, Chance stresses in his 9to5Mac review, but you “almost never” notice it visually unless you’re looking for it – just like most Android foldables. He adds that you’re more likely to feel it than see it. 

The app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet. That’s what pushed Android foldables into the “phone that turns into a square tablet” trend they were stuck in for years, despite brands like Oppo and Google coming up with this iPhone Duo form factor way before Apple was a part of the conversation. Apple has the same problem, and it’s not going to be fixed overnight.

That said, it’s clear that it’s going to get cleaned up much quicker. WIRED‘s review opens up mentioning how “in the past day” key apps including “Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.”

“Mr Foldable” himself, Michael Fisher, explains in his review how apps that are not optimized are rough, comparing it to the early days of iPad, but that some key players are already stepping up. On top of that, smaller devs are building apps clearly inspired of this new form factor. “Tiny Computers” looks absolutely delightful.

David Imel mentions that “you can scale things up and they work, but they do look silly” in regards to unoptimized apps, and also makes a good point – not everything is going to get updated. iOS apps that aren’t actively maintained anymore are always going to be a mess on this device and, frankly, the scaling features Apple gives you make everything look way worse than an unoptimized app on an Android foldable has ever looked.

Look at the options you get for the yet-to-be-optimized Google Maps. Michael Fisher points out how it still doesn’t take up the whole display and that, if you rotate the phone, it just sends you back to square one. Sounds bad!

Apple’s new sidebar UI, which I still think looks funky, is personally my biggest fear as these wide foldable form factors take over, not because it’s a bad idea – Fisher points out that he actually loves it – but because Android apps will probably take a whole lot longer to adopt it. Seeing where things are starting out on the iPhone Duo, yeah, I’m sticking with that take.

That outer display, too, seems to be a hang up. The Verge says that “most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time.” That’s a problem I ran into a bit with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its similar shout and stout form factor, but Apple’s device is even smaller, so I’m not shocked to hear this. 

That same review makes a case for Apple’s app split, saying that “the problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time,” while saying that “the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them.” I’m not sure I agree there – larger canvases and multitasking alone have sold me on a foldable for years – but seeing so many iOS apps going all-in on the new screen size certainly has me feeling a bit envious. 

Another review that caught my eye was from Joanna Stern, where she puts the iPhone Duo “through hell.” There are two things of note here. First, Joanna puts the Duo through over 32,000 folds on top of normal daily use, and the hinge unsurprisingly holds up well. Android brands have laid an incredible foundation here, so even if Apple took its own route, the technology is clearly up to par here for a strong foldable hinge. 

But also pointed out here is a problem that’s been on every single Android foldable I’ve ever used – the iPhone Duo gets warm. Joanna calls the device a “hand warmer” and, apparently, Apple said this was business as usual for the device’s heat management. I was curious if the thicker design of Duo would help alleviate this one, but it seems Apple is dealing with the same issue. It’s a lot harder to cool two halves of a device, and you feel that heat more when there’s more usable space on the device.

Virtually every review mentions how hefty the iPhone Duo’s hardware is, too. This is a problem that Android foldables have been chipping away at generation-by-generation, and that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the poster child for. Smartphone weight continues to be something you don’t notice until it pushes over the edge and, while we’re not at Pixel Fold levels, iPhone Duo is very much at that edge.

Based on these early reviews, Apple didn’t reinvent the foldable, but it’s clear there’s a level of polish on the iPhone Duo that was lacking on Android foldables. Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start. 

What’s next for Android foldables? I look forward to seeing exactly that…

title: Leaker reveals larger iPhone Duo details, possible Telephoto camera
snippet: Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera. more…
fullText:
Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera.

Mark Gurman details Apple’s plans for larger iPhone Duo, says Telephoto is ‘on their list’ for future models

The iPhone Duo isn’t yet available in stores, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman already has plenty to share about Apple’s plans for future models.

Today on his Power On podcast, Gurman revealed that Apple is testing iPhone Duo 2 models with Face ID under the outer display, and is exploring ways to add an Action button. You can read more about those details here.

Later in the episode, Gurman looks further out to a 2028 third-gen model that he’s previously reported on.

The iPhone Duo 3 is expected to be slightly larger, and on the podcast Gurman offered specifics on what to expect. He said:

What I heard, just to be specific about the larger screen version of the Duo, is I heard…it’s marginal. It would be that the bigger screen, or the inside screen, increasing by, it’s like, this is rough, like very roughly half an inch. And so, that wouldn’t necessarily make the outer screen much bigger…we’re not talking about an 8.5-inch, 9-inch inner screen. We’re talking about like high sevens, very low eights.

For reference, iPhone Duo currently has a 7.6-inch folding display.

	

Gurman compares the forthcoming change to how Apple gradually sized up its Pro line in recent years. For example, it went from 6.7 inches on iPhone 15 Pro Max to 6.9 inches on iPhone 16 Pro Max.

As part of the conversation, Gurman is also asked if Apple is going to add a Telephoto camera to a future iPhone Duo. He says, “That’s on their list. I don’t know when that’s coming, but that’s gonna be hard to do.” 

He adds that it isn’t a matter of cost, but physics: “I think that’s purely a physics issue in terms of the depth needed. It’s going to be interesting to see how they end up solving that.”

title: YouTube Is Letting Us Vibe Our Video Feeds, and I’m Liking It
snippet: The mobile app is giving users more control of the videos they get.
fullText:
Let’s face it — we love scrolling through videos. Maybe you’re OK with what YouTube feeds you, maybe you’re not. Either way, you’ve now got more control over it.

YouTube this week added a feature to the mobile app home page that enables you to create your own video feeds for whatever topics you want. The feed helps you home in on the subjects that appeal to you instead of necessarily relying on the algorithm. The custom feed option appears as a plus sign on the horizontal menu at the top of the app’s home screen.

YouTube said in its announcement that it wants to help users “dive straight into” their favorite content. “We know that viewers come to YouTube with incredibly unique interests, moods, topics to explore, and favorite ways to watch,” the YouTube team said.

			

More from CNET

The horizontal menu is also new. It includes tabs for your custom feeds, subscribed channels, music and live streams. There’s also a Music & TV button for people who subscribe to YouTube TV or Primetime Channels.

To see it for yourself, go to the app’s home screen on your phone. At the top, you’ll see the menu. If you click on Subs, you’ll see your subscribed channels. The Music tab will show videos from your favorite artists, and the Live button will show livestreams from your favorite creators. The More button shows a menu of YouTube features.

Trying out the new YouTube settings

But the most intriguing addition was the custom feed feature, and I gave it a go. On the YouTube home screen menu, I clicked on the plus sign. Then, under the “Add a custom feed for any topic or mood,” I typed San Francisco 49ers, and voila, a new tab appeared on the menu — SF 49ers. I also added a feed for the 2026 midterm elections. Both of those feeds now appear in the menu.

You can create a YouTube video feed for any topic.YouTube

You can also modify or delete a feed. If you click into a feed, you’ll see buttons at the top to edit the prompt, rename the feed or delete the feed.

I decided to modify my 49ers feed. Since I’m also a fan of the Golden State Warriors NBA team, I changed the feed topic to include both the 49ers and the Warriors. That feed then showed videos for both teams.

For non-Premium users, you get three feeds. You get up to eight if you subscribe to YouTube Premium ($9 per month).

The custom feed feature was already available on desktop — added by YouTube last month. It’s not yet available on tablets, and YouTube owner Google hasn’t said when it will be.

You must be 13 or older to get the custom feeds feature, and you also must have both watch and search history enabled.

title: You should pick up this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL over its $1,300 sequel
snippet: Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon.

It’s no secret that consumer tech prices are continuing to balloon in the face of AI-driven RAM shortages, which makes any deal on last-gen tech always worth considering. It says a lot that, even removed from that context, this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL in Moonstone remains an all-around great deal, saving you a whopping $450 over its successor without much in the way of meaningful sacrifices. In fact, considering the 256GB variant actually has more RAM than this year’s base Pro XL model, you might come out ahead in the long run.

Buy Pixel 10 Pro XL for $850 at Amazon

Still, it’s worth breaking some of those sacrifices down. In addition to the obvious downside of losing a year’s worth of software upgrades — since we’re a full 12 months further along the Pixel 10’s seven-year lifecycle — you’ll have to be willing to lose a handful of changes on both the hardware and software fronts. Other hardware changes include a Tensor G5 over the G6, a slightly dimmer display, a smaller telephoto sensor, and, of course, the lack of everybody’s favorite underbaked Google feature, HiLight.

But hey, at least you get a temperature sensor and a brighter flash.

On the software side, Camera Looks is the big missing tool, with no plans to bring my favorite Pixel camera feature to previous generations on the horizon. However, I wouldn’t say Camera Looks is worth the extra $450, especially when Camera Looks being backported certainly remains a possibility in play. The same goes for Google’s typical slate of AI features; tools like Rambler remain Pixel 11-exclusive for now, but considering third-party developers have already made their own moves in this regard, I would expect to see an improved take on the company’s latest voice-to-text model show up sooner rather than later.

	

Don’t sleep on this deal; we’ve already seen a $700 sale price for the smaller Pixel 10 Pro in 256GB sell out (though the 128GB model is still available for $750). If you’re looking for a new phone to help you weather RAMageddon — and you don’t want to break the bank to buy it — this Pixel 10 Pro XL might be your best hope.

fullText:
Google TV is rolling out its latest feature roundup, showcasing new features and additions that have rolled out in recent months.

Next time you turn on your Google TV, you might be greeted with the October 2026 roundup of new feature additions. Google has been sending out these occasional fullscreen summaries for a while, with the latest showing up this week on Google TV Streamer and other devices.

The new features Google is highlighting this month include:

New Freeplay channels & on-demand content

Watchlist relocation & tweaks

Google Photos search

Gemini-aided “Remix your photos”

Dynamic slideshows

These have mostly rolled out over the past few months. 

	
	

We clocked the new Freeplay channels last month, with Google TV now offering over 300 built-in channels. The expansion of free on-demand movies and shows was announced in August and rolled out shortly after. Dynamic slideshows launched back in April, and Photo search even further back in January.

The new Watchlist location change arrived in a homescreen redesign back in November of last year.

All is to say, your guess is as good as ours as to why Google chose to showcase these features as “new” right now, when realistically there’s only one new addition in tow. It’s not the first time this has happened, with these roundups showing up a couple of times a year on Google TV Streamer and other devices, but it’s certainly something to see such a broad window of what’s considered “new.”

fullText:
Lindsay Powell, who releases records under the name Fielded, has spent most of her career subverting expectations and genre conventions. According to their Bandcamp page, Fielded started as an experimental noise project before growing into something closer to R&B. But from moment one, her take on the genre was restless, relentlessly playing with what R&B even means.

Her first album, Ninety-Thirty-Thirty, includes songs heavily indebted to ’80s synth-pop and features multiple saxophone solos. Boy Angel is a quirky electronic exploration with huge saw-wave synths, jittery percussion, and sky-high vocal stacks. While 2020’s Demisexual Lovelace is a slinkier affair, released on underground hip-hop imprint Backwoodz Studioz and features contributions from Billy Woods and Elucid (Armand Hammer).

Her latest record, Some Kind of Animal, pulls from all of these various versions of Fielded, placing organ-fueled slow jams like “That Bitch” next to a cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Closer” that has strong 2000s neo-soul vibes, as well as the industrial funk of “Heaven,” which includes a guest verse from Pink Siifu.

We wanted to know what’s behind Fielded’s genre-defying madness.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My most indispensable tool in recording is my Universal Audio Apollo Twin audio interface. I love its ease of function and I love the Universal Audio digital studio plugins. I use them on all of my records during the recording process and beyond. I can mic up and get a professional sound in no time, plus my guitars and synths sound amazing and clear.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

Right now I have a pirated full-length version of the Japanese cyberpunk film 964 Pinocchio pinned to my tab bar for endless sonic and visual inspiration.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

I don’t know if it is a tech trend or a plague, but I deeply wish AI would disappear off of the face of the earth.

What creation are you most proud of?

I am most proud of my latest album Some Kind of Animal, specifically the single of the same title, and thank goddess for that; I’d be bummed if my favorite musical output was in the rearview.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

The best piece of advice I’ve ever received, throughout my whole life, is to be patient. Everything happens in perfect time; there is no reason to be jealous or envious because our journeys are completely our own and everything happens for a reason. What is meant for us will come for us, and what is not meant for us should be metabolized as a lesson that helps us grow and become exactly who we are meant to be.

What is your current obsession?

I am currently obsessed with stories about scammers. All stories about all scammers; big scams, small scams, scams that ended in minor jail time or a blow-out of incredible impact. I love scammers, and I am fascinated by their brains.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

The last piece of physical media I bought was Alissa Bennett’s compilation of essays entitled Taxidermist’s Handbook, full of — you guessed it — stories about scammers (amongst other types of criminals).

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Freak Today, Freak Tomorrow.

title: iPhone Duo has a bigger battery than Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold.

The iPhone Duo measures in at 254g and is 11.3mm thick when closed. That’s considerably heavier and a fair bit thicker than virtually every other Android foldable on the market today, as we previously discussed.

iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable

But Apple isn’t wasting that space.

Despite the short and stout footprint of the iPhone Duo, the device is packing a 4,883 mAh battery. That’s the rated capacity as confirmed on an EU energy label, that is, as Apple almost never publicly confirms the battery capacity of iPhones. MacRumors did find the same info on Apple’s own documentation of the same EU energy label.

	

That’s not exactly a huge number in the foldable space, but it’s bigger than the iPhone Duo’s main competitor offers. Citing the same EU data, here’s how Samsung and Google compared:

iPhone Duo: 4,883 mAh

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: 4,854 mAh

Galaxy Z Fold 8: 4,660 mAh

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 4,658 mAh

Ouch.

Neither the Fold 8 nor the Pixel 11 Pro Fold have particularly bad battery life, but Apple having a bigger battery along with the host of other reasons that iPhone users are in Apple’s ecosystem makes it harder to convince anyone to look at Samsung or Google’s devices – the main competitors in the US – as a complete alternative to the Duo.

What do you think?

iPhone Duo pre-orders are already delayed well into 2027.

title: Apple exploring fix for Safari’s cramped layout on the iPhone Duo’s outer display
snippet: In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details.

Apple knows Safari isn’t making full use of iPhone Duo’s outer display

One issue singled out in multiple iPhone Duo reviews (including ours) was the fact that Safari’s right-aligned controls take up a significant portion of the outer display’s limited screen space, leaving websites with an unusually narrow area to show their content.

Here’s what Chance Miller had to say about this in his review, published earlier this week:

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

[…]

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen.

For new iPhone Duo users who have also been frustrated by this issue, Apple’s Jen Simmons shared some good news today.

In a post highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, including how websites adapt to the iPhone Duo’s different screen sizes and folding positions, Simmons acknowledged that websites currently can’t extend behind the controls on the device’s outer display, and said Apple is exploring ways to address that limitation.

	

From her post:

We would like to give web designers and developers the ability to design and use that space in more creative ways. Perhaps you want to extend your header background across the full width of the display, for example. It might seem like there’s just one obvious way to make this possible, but really there are many possibilities.

Simmons went on to explain that simply using the HTML viewport meta tag with viewport-fit="cover" to extend websites behind Safari’s controls could cause problems, because many websites don’t properly account for those areas, potentially leaving important content obscured.

Instead, she invited developers to share their ideas as Apple explores a better approach:

We are investigating if there’s a better way to accomplish the same result — something more foolproof and perhaps easier for you to use. If you have ideas, we’d love to hear them. And stay tuned.

If you’re a web developer and have ideas on how Apple could address this limitation, you can read the full WebKit post for details on how to share your feedback.

fullText:
Across several decades in Hollywood, Caleb Deschanel has seen a lot. He served as cinematographer on films like The Passion of the Christ and The Patriot, worked on sequences in The Godfather and Titanic, and directed a few episodes of Twin Peaks. Even still, nothing could quite prepare him for his first stop-motion project: working as the cinematographer on Wildwood, the latest release from Coraline studio Laika. While he knew that stop-motion was a long and involved process, he was still surprised by just how much work went into these movies. “When I started I thought it was one thing, and then I quickly found out that it was another thing,” Deschanel says. “It was much more complicated than I expected.”

Wildwood has been a long time coming. Laika CEO Travis Knight originally optioned the rights for the book of the same name, written by Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, in 2011. But production didn’t begin until a decade later. “I’ve been working on it in some form or another for 16 years,” Knight, who also directed Wildwood, says. “The reason why I stuck with it, the reason why I had to make this movie no matter what, is because of what it meant to me personally. Underneath it all, it’s a story about love and loss and grief, it’s about the impossible things that love asks of us, and that meant something to me personally in a very profound way.”

It’s also the biggest production Laika has ever undertaken. Wildwood tells the story of a young girl named Prue who has to venture into the “impassable wilderness” that surrounds Portland in order to find her baby brother. When she enters the forest she discovers a fantasy realm reminiscent of Narnia, with magical spells, talking animals, and warring factions. It required nearly 50 animators and more than 200 puppets to pull it off, and the film is full of ambitious sequences, like a 12-minute battle with dozens of soldiers and a chase scene through a bustling Portland, where Prue’s brother is carried away by a gigantic murder of crows.

Image: Laika

Image: Laika

According to head of animation Brad Schiff, the studio’s ethos involves mixing “old-school craft with modern technology.” With each project, he says, Laika develops new techniques. If something works well, they then push the idea even further on the next project. For instance, on Laika’s previous film, Missing Link, the main character was outfitted with a diaphragm so that when an animator turned a screw on the puppet’s back, the diaphragm could expand or contract, creating the illusion that it was breathing. This has since become the standard for puppets in Laika’s films.

These may sound like small details, but over the years they add up. For costume designer Deb Cook, there wasn’t a single innovation on Wildwood that stood out to her, but rather the sheer number of tools she had at her disposal. “Over time we’ve gathered together a library of techniques that we’ve been able to put into practice on this movie,” she says. This was especially important on Wildwood, which features a huge range of costumes; in the city sequences everyone is dressed in modern clothing, whereas in the forest characters have more fantastical looks.

“It was much more complicated than I expected.”

For Wildwood, many of the advancements came down to materials. The costumes made use of more flexible fabrics, for example, and the team also engineered a new process for creating silicone that’s lighter and more durable than what they previously used. “We’ve done this so we can wean ourselves off of foam latex, which is stinky and it shrinks over time, and five years later it kind of just crumbles,” says Oliver Jones, head of characters and practical effects. “There are advantages to rethinking a lot of these materials that were our go-to probably since King Kong.”

The scale of Wildwood has also forced the studio to adopt another seemingly much more boring practice: being better organized. “They’ve been misplaced,” Cook says, when asked if she’s ever lost a puppet. “There’s now a very sophisticated tracking system because there are so many moving parts, and so many stages around the studio.”

And while much has been said about the large and elaborate sequences in the film — Knight says the epic battle scene is “probably the most technically challenging thing that we’ve ever done” — all of these techniques are designed to imbue more humanity into characters that are portrayed by puppets. In that regard, small details like the flow of fabric or the impression of breathing are vitally important.

Image: Laika

Image: Laika

“We also have really subtle and intimate scenes, quiet scenes that don’t have a lot of flash, that have virtually no sound design or music, where the only thing that you’re experiencing is the grief of a father talking about a secret that he’s been holding on to for 15 years, or a quiet moment of a woman grieving the loss of her son,” Knight explains. “These are moments where you have nowhere to hide and the performances of these little puppets — these little assemblages of steel and silicon and fabric that have no life of their own — completely spring to life because of the hand and the artistry of the human behind it. Those are the moments that I’m most proud of.”

In this way, the long road to Wildwood hitting theaters makes a lot of sense. Laika has been around for just over 20 years, and over the course of each film the studio has innovated to steadily push its craft forward. Knight may have been thinking about the film for 16 years, but creating the version that is coming out in 2026 wouldn’t have been possible without all of the learnings spread across films like ParaNorman and Kubo and the Two Strings.

For Knight, it’s been especially gratifying to bring it to life with a team of both Laika veterans and newcomers, including not only Deschanel but also a handful of young animators for whom Wildwood was their first feature film project. Some were young enough that Coraline, Laika’s very first film, was what inspired them to get into the field in the first place. “I was really moved by that,” says Knight. “It also made me feel old as shit.”

Wildwood is in theaters now.

He served as cinematographer on films like The Passion of the Christ and The Patriot, worked on sequences in The Godfather and Titanic, and directed a few episodes of Twin Peaks. Even still, nothing could quite prepare him for his first stop-motion project: working as the cinematographer on Wildwood, the latest release from Coraline studio Laika. While he knew that stop-motion was a long and involved process, he was still surprised by just how much work went into these movies. “When I started I thought it was one thing, and then I quickly found out that it was another thing,” Deschanel says. “It was much more complicated than I expected.”

title: Man Destroys $2,000 iPhone Duo With Dirt, Fire, Knives and Medieval Chainmail
snippet: YouTuber JerryRigEverything tests the iPhone Duo’s durability for scratch and dust resistance. And it is wild to watch.
fullText:
It might seem obvious, but try not to sit on your iPhone Duo when you leave it open.

That lesson comes a day after Apple’s foldable iPhone hit stores with lines of people queued up to buy the new device. Tech reviewer Zach Nelson dropped an iPhone Duo video on his YouTube channel, JerryRigEverything, testing the scratch resistance and bendability of the new $2,000 phone. 

Let’s just say that Nelson’s measured, soothing voice didn’t keep me calm as he meticulously destroyed the Duo.

			

More from CNET

He subjected it to numerous scratch tests on both its cover and inner screens. Nelson praised Apple for the cover screen’s Ceramic Shield 2 glass and noted that the inner screen, even with its nano-texture finish, scratches as easily as the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s nonmatte folding display.

But why stop there?

Nelson used medieval chainmail (no proof it was actually from the Middle Ages), dirt, dust and pebbles to test the Duo further. Surprisingly, the new phone handled the chainmail easily. Nelson partly credits that to the Duo’s matte finish on the inner screen, which seems to hide imperfections. 

He then opened the Duo’s inner screen and tried to bend it backward a few times. As you might expect, the frame flexed, which led to cracks showing up on the main 7.6-inch screen. So if you set your Duo down with its main screen open on a chair or couch, just don’t sit on it.

In a review by CNET senior technology reporter Abrar Al-Heeti, Al-Heeti recommends protecting the Duo, saying, “You should probably still get a case and AppleCare, or be prepared to pay a pretty penny for repairs.”

You can watch Nelson’s video to see the entire nearly 15-minute video. Warning: the dust and dirt portion against the Duo’s hinge is psychologically difficult to witness (because of all the dust and dirt). Also, if you’re wondering more about the iPhone Duo’s durability, CNET has designed and constructed a custom machine called the Fold-a-Phone that is currently hard at work testing how many times Apple’s foldable can be open and closed.

title: Gemini Notebook now available as Connected App for deeper integration
snippet: Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration. more…
fullText:
Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration.

As a Connected App like Google Workspace or Photos, @Gemini Notebook “allows you to manage and query notebooks directly within your chats using natural language.”

This integration lets you retrieve information from existing notebooks, create new ones, add sources, and save notes. The Gemini app will “automatically detect when to use the Gemini Notebook Connected App for relevant prompts.” For example: 

Create, edit, or delete a notebook (“Create a Gemini Notebook about solar farm market trends”)

Add, update, or delete sources in a notebook (“Add a copy of this chat to my notebook about Bio 101 course”)

List notebooks and their sources (“Show me a list of all the sources in my notebook about US National Parks”)

Answer questions using context from your notebook (“What do my Gemini Notebooks say about butterfly migration?”)

This integration is available now and has been enabled by “default for users globally, except in the European Economic Area, where it will be OFF by default.”

	

@Gemini Notebook is “available to all Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
snippet: After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all. more…
fullText:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.

Update 10/22: YouTube has confirmed this is not a public-facing test.

YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening

In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts, YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.

A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.

	

It’s not the only case of this happening, though.

	

Over the past couple of weeks, reports on Reddit have seen the dislike button vanish, with another web user seeing a slightly different UI to the one above, but with the same result of offloading the button to an overflow menu alongside the “Report” button. 

YouTube runs tests like this frequently, but given the same change was made to the dislike button on Shorts several months ago, it’s all but certain that the same will happen to standard videos.

What do you think of the change?

More on YouTube:

YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium

YouTube begins rolling out GIF support for comments very slowly; it’s for a reason

title: iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, here’s what’s coming
snippet: iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming.

Messages

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Apple TV

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

FaceTime

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Home

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now being split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

	

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple Podcasts the big fix I’ve wanted for years

Games

Apple’s Games app has a couple smaller upgrades for its Home tab in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

title: 7 iPhone Duo Apps That Take Full Advantage of the New Foldable Phone
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo brings iOS to a bigger tablet-like display, and these creative apps are already optimized to make the most of it.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is easily the most experimental iPhone that Apple has released. That’s both good news and bad news.

On one hand, the shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos.

		

			

On the other hand, the device is so new to iOS that some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s getting an iPhone Duo today (or soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested. 

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent. 

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantasical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo.Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster. 

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-sized phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other. 

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

							Contributor

He has over 10 years of experience testing and reviewing consumer technology from mobile hardware to home entertainment.

title: Google Health 5.11 rolling out with Fitbit Air Health Guardian, improved sleep tracking, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.

The Improved Automatic Activity Tracking is available now for the Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5, with the Fitbit Edge getting the capabilities at launch on October 27.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to up to 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, we now factor in more context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half.2

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to the Google Health app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

The Fitbit Air and Edge are getting two Health Guardian features if you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber. You can set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends now, with the first report available at the beginning of November.

Blood pressure trends, which allow you to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart, will be available in the Health Guardian section of the Health tab if you’ve worn your Fitbit Air for 5 or more consecutive days in October.

Insulin resistance trends, which track monthly shifts in your metabolic health, will be available if you’ve worn your watch for 7 or more days and nights in October.

Blood glucose is now “Glucose” throughout the Google Health app with updated charts and graphs. Additionally:

	

Custom time-in-range goals: You can now set specific time-in-range goals for glucose data from connected continuous glucose monitors. To set a goal, go to the Metabolic section of the Health tab, tap Glucose, open Settings, and select Set goal.

Faster syncing with Lingo by Abbott (US only): You can now connect Lingo by Abbott directly to the Google Health app so your glucose data syncs faster — displaying in the Google Health app within 30 minutes of a reading. If you have a Google Health Premium membership, Google Health Coach³ can also answer questions about your glucose trends. To connect, tap your profile icon in the Google Health app and select Partner Apps.³

Finally, there’s improved Sleep Tracking across wake detection and nap editing:

More accurate awake detection: We’ve improved our sleep tracking to better factor in your steps data so that we can more accurately track short awakenings, like getting up to use the bathroom. 

Easier nap editing: You’re always in control of your sleep data. If a nap ever shows up that doesn’t match your day, you can now easily remove it directly from your nap card.

Version 5.11 is available on iOS and still rolling out for Android users.

snippet: Crowds camped outside of stores before Apple’s first folding phone became available.
fullText:
Apple’s causing a commotion with its new iPhone Duo. 

The tech giant’s first foldable phone hit shelves Friday, and lines were forming (and selling out) well before Apple stores even opened. Many preordered the phone, but that didn’t stop people from trying their luck to buy one without an order number. CNET editors and reporters were on the ground to bring you all of the uproar, so you can save yourself the trip if you were trying to buy one over the weekend.

At Apple’s flagship 5th Avenue location in New York, the line started forming on Wednesday by 9 a.m. ET — two days before the launch. Over 50 people were waiting in line by Thursday at 7 p.m. ET, sometimes with buckets serving as placeholders. In the first minutes after the store opened, there was no word that the iPhone Duo had sold out yet, but other stores were sold out before their doors opened.

The Oxmoor Center opened at 6 a.m. ET for Apple fans planning to buy the iPhone Duo on launch day. Faith Chihil/CNET

At the Oxmoor Center in Louisville, Kentucky, the Apple store opened at 8 a.m. EDT, and CNET’s Faith Chihil saw a line of more than 40 people three hours earlier. At about 7:27 a.m. ET, Apple store employees started taking orders for the phone. But the 256GB iPhone Duo was already sold out.

		

			

Lines gather outside of Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, where the iPhone Duo sold out before 7:30 a.m. ET.David Katzmaier / CNET

CNET Editor in Chief David Katzmaier reported that the first person was in line at Walt Whitman Shops in Huntington, New York, on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET, and was able to preorder the phone. Apple store employees started taking orders to pick up the phone at 7 a.m. ET.  But by 7:30 a.m. ET, the rest of the line was dismissed after an announcement that the store had sold out before doors opened.

CNET’s Patrick Holland reported from Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco. The first people started forming a line at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday. As of 11 a.m. ET, lines were down the block and around the building. There were also some sightings of people reselling the iPhone Duo just moments after waiting in line to buy one.

The line for the iPhone Duo started at 9:30 p.m. ET on Thursday at Apple’s Union Square store in San Francisco.Patrick Holland / CNET

Meanwhile, at the Apple store at University Village in Seattle, about 180 people were waiting in line who didn’t preorder the iPhone Duo. It sold out within 15 minutes of the store opening.

While many may have expected new Apple CEO John Ternus to be at the New York flagship store, he debuted the iPhone Duo launch at the Apple store in Austin, Texas. He might have been there because of this weekend’s Formula 1 race in the city — streaming on Apple TV.

iPhone Duo buyers had ‘one more thing’ waiting at pickup

Apple is full of surprises. In line with the company’s “one more thing” tagline, those who preordered the iPhone Duo had a surprise awaiting them at unboxing.

Apple’s usual “Hello” welcome screen included their name when they first turned on the phone. It’s clearly a special detail the company thought of before today, and it’s the first time it has customized its usual welcome screen for customers.

Jean Vasquez, founder of True Skies, shows off his iPhone Duo with his name on the opening screen. Bridget Carey / CNET

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable iPhone, debuted earlier this month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It features split-screen capabilities, a photo preview display, Touch ID instead of Face ID and Apple Pencil support. The iPhone Duo’s preorders opened on Oct. 16, but quickly turned into a backlog that stretches into early next year. Pricing starts at $1,999.

“Details like the matte inner display, under-display inner camera and smooth transitions between screens give the Duo a premium feel that helps to justify its high price tag, at least to some extent,” CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti said in her review of the iPhone Duo.

The Duo, Al-Heeti said, “is a foldable experience that feels cohesive, intuitive and genuinely useful, which could help win over more people to foldables in general. But I think that broader appeal is still a ways off.”

We don’t know how many iPhone Duos are available at each store or when Apple will restock its physical locations. But there’s a limit of two iPhone Duos per person, per day, which marks the first time in a long time that Apple’s put a cap on how many you can buy. 

If you’re set on getting the phone, try ordering on Apple’s website and picking it up at a nearby store to get the phone sooner, but you’ll need to check availability on Oct. 24. It could be sooner than its estimated shipping times that say the phone won’t arrive until Jan. 29 in some areas.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Dashia Milden
						

						

							Senior Consumer Insights Editor						
					

											

								

											Dashia is the consumer insights editor for CNET. She specializes in data-driven analysis and news at the intersection of tech, personal finance and consumer sentiment. Dashia investigates economic shifts and everyday challenges to help readers make well-informed decisions, and she covers a range of topics, including technology, security, energy and money. title: New App Store chief discusses Apple’s gaming strategy, future of Apple Arcade, more
snippet: In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said. more…
fullText:
In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said.

New App Store chief talks App Store gaming

Apple’s ambitions to be seen as a proper gaming platform owner aren’t exactly new. Over the years, the company has repeatedly attempted to attract major game developers and convince players to take gaming on its devices more seriously, with varying degrees of success.

And those efforts show. As Apple has repeatedly highlighted during WWDC keynotes and product announcements, the company has introduced hardware-accelerated ray tracing, made significant improvements to its Metal graphics framework, and developed tools that make it easier to port PC and console games to its platforms.

Early last week, shortly after Carson Oliver’s promotion to vice president of the App Store was reported, Apple announced Indie Games Week, highlighting seven new and upcoming games for iPhone and iPad, including:

Sifu

Vampire Crawlers

No Man’s Sky

Little Kitty, Big City

9 Kings

Dome Keeper

Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall

In light of that, Polygon conducted an email interview with Oliver, who shared some interesting details about the state of gaming on the App Store and Apple’s plans for the future.

Oliver told Polygon:

“We’ve seen incredible growth of games coming to the App Store, in general, with more premium games releasing on the App Store this year than last. […] While many of those are indies, we’re also seeing more console and PC franchises coming to mobile, as it is a burgeoning audience for those games. These seven games featured in Indie Games Week capture where gaming on iPhone and iPad is heading: incredible diversity and creativity with no compromises on quality.”

Oliver also touched on the technical improvements Apple has made over the years, some of which we mentioned above, as well as the role that younger generations of players have had in shaping the mobile gaming market.

According to Oliver, “an entire generation of players” grew up with an iPhone as their first gaming device, rather than a traditional console or PC.

He added:

“These users embrace direct touch as their primary controller, making iPhone and iPad the ultimate canvas for indie innovation.”

As for Apple Arcade, and how it fits into Apple’s broader gaming strategy alongside the growing number of premium games launching directly on the App Store, Oliver told Polygon it comes down to giving game developers more flexibility:

“We want to give developers a trusted place to reach users around the world, support them at each stage, and help them build successful businesses. […] To achieve that goal, we provide developers with flexible business model options. That means a breakthrough phenomenon like Balatro can thrive as a premium download, and it can also find a home as part of the Apple Arcade service. The important thing is that we give developers the flexibility to make the best choice for every game and players the freedom to play how they want.”

To read Oliver’s full interview with Polygon, which also touches on App Store discoverability, and the types of games finding success on Apple’s platforms, follow this link.
